title: Narayan, 1009: Mahmud’s raid, an elephant tribute, and a coerced peace
excerpt: Al-Utbi records killing, plunder, and the overthrow of sacred images at Narayan, followed by a bargain for elephants, soldiers, and safe caravans. The location and the identity of the negotiating ruler require care.
html:
After the riches seized at Nagarkot had been displayed at Ghazna, Mahmud led another expedition into northern India. Its destination appears in al-Utbi’s account as Narain or Narayan. The narrative is brief, but its consequences are explicit: chiefs defeated, sacred images overthrown, people killed, property taken, and a subsequent agreement promising elephants and soldiers to the conqueror. The same account ends with caravans travelling safely between Hind and Khurasan. Violence and commerce appear within a few paragraphs of each other.[1]

This campaign forms part of the guide to Mahmud’s invasions. It follows the Waihind and Nagarkot expedition of 1008–1009. It must remain distinct from the Nandana campaign of 1013–1014: similar place names and confusing translated headings have repeatedly brought these separate episodes together.

A campaign after Nagarkot

The preceding expedition had combined victory over Shahi resistance with the seizure of devotional wealth at a hill fortress associated with Nagarkot. Al-Utbi describes the treasures being shown to foreign envoys at Ghazna. His transition to Narayan therefore places the new attack within an already established pattern: military success abroad became royal display at home. Wealth was transported, presented, distributed, and made to demonstrate the ruler’s exceptional standing.[1]

Narayan was not another name for the same fortress. The court chronicler introduces a fresh expedition and then a separate embassy. He does not supply a full itinerary, departure date, or list of the towns crossed. Muhammad Nazim’s twentieth-century reconstruction dates the attack to the beginning of 400 AH, approximately October 1009, using the order in al-Utbi and the dating supplied by Ibn al-Athir. The latter wrote substantially later. The date is a reasoned reconstruction rather than an exact day recorded by a campaign eyewitness.[2]

There is also a contemporary poetic reference. Nazim cites a verse attributed to Ghadāʾiri celebrating a reward received for the victory of Narayan. It supports the place of the victory in courtly patronage, although it cannot supply the missing military itinerary. A poet’s reward and a chronicler’s account illuminate the royal publicity surrounding success; neither gives the defending population’s own record of the attack.[2]

Where was Narayan?

Modern reconstructions commonly identify the destination with Narayanpur in the Alwar region of Rajasthan. Nazim follows Alexander Cunningham’s identification and connects the expedition with access toward the Ganges plain. That location is useful for understanding the usual historical reconstruction, but it should be labelled as an identification, not treated as a coordinate printed in al-Utbi’s text.[2]

The nineteenth-century discussion in Elliot and Dowson is less settled. Its editors considered a connection with Anhilwara and acknowledged geographical difficulties. Their appendix is valuable because it preserves the uncertainty, even when its proposed solutions have not stood equally well. An old translation’s footnote is not another medieval witness to the location.[3]

Al-Utbi says Mahmud reached the middle of Hind. That expression cannot fix the site on a modern map. The chronicler’s geographical language centres the conqueror’s advance and the scope of his success; it is not a measured survey of the subcontinent. A precise route passing through a sequence of present-day districts would need evidence beyond this phrase.

The distinction from Nandana is firmer than the exact location of Narayan. In the Arabic-derived extracts translated by Elliot and Dowson, Narain appears on printed page 36 and Nardin on pages 37–39. They are separated by an embassy and belong to different points in the narrative. Reynolds’s translation of a Persian adaptation uses headings that can obscure that distinction. The later Salt Range fighting should not be moved to Rajasthan simply because names look alike in English transliteration.[1][2][4]

What the original narrative actually records

Al-Utbi describes Mahmud marching over hard and soft ground until he reaches the country of chiefs who had previously acknowledged no master. The description is politically revealing. Independence itself becomes a condition the invading ruler is entitled to end. The narrative measures success through the reduction of these chiefs and the destruction of the religious objects under their protection.[1]

The source reports a battle, plunder in property, horses, and elephants, and killing across hills and valleys. It does not give a dependable overall death toll. Nor does it provide a sequence of named defenders, a siege duration, or a detailed account of the main town’s fall. Those omissions limit what can be reconstructed. The supported narrative is already severe without adding invented street fighting, civilian speeches, or a specific number of dead.[1]

The overthrow of images was part of the action the chronicler celebrated. Describing the campaign only as a commercial opening would erase that statement. Describing it only as image-breaking would erase the simultaneous seizure of wealth, military animals, and political authority. The source presents these outcomes together because each could reinforce the prestige and resources of the ruler.

Its language also divides people into the conqueror’s religious community and a despised opposition. Such labels tell us how a Ghaznavid court writer justified the violence. They are not neutral descriptions of the inhabitants. We can report the killing directly without adopting the author’s judgment that the victims’ beliefs made their deaths meritorious.

The embassy that followed

After the raid, al-Utbi introduces an embassy from a ruler of Hind who had witnessed the devastation caused by conflict with Mahmud. Relatives and chiefs were sent to ask that further invasions cease. Their offer included an annual delivery of fifty elephants, products of the country, and two thousand men for service at Mahmud’s court.[1]

The identification of this ruler needs care. Al-Utbi does not provide a personal name in the passage. Nazim understands him as the ruler of Narayanpur, while nineteenth-century editors made other connections. The natural sequence makes a connection with the preceding raid plausible, but the text does not permit a confident biography of the negotiator. An account should preserve the distinction between the named destination and the unnamed ruler of the embassy.[1][2][3]

This was an agreement negotiated under the threat of renewed invasion. The ruler’s offer followed reported destruction in his country and concern for his subjects. Calling it simply a friendly exchange would conceal the pressure that made the bargain possible. Equally, the text does not say Mahmud abolished the negotiating court or replaced every local institution with direct Ghaznavid administration. Tribute could leave an existing ruler in place while imposing a costly subordinate relationship.

Al-Utbi says Mahmud accepted the offer and sent an envoy to ensure that its conditions were carried out. A vassal of the Indian ruler accompanied the elephants to Ghazna. These details show that the agreement involved verification and delivery, not merely a declaration in a victory speech. Nevertheless, the account does not supply a surviving treaty, a year-by-year register of payments, or evidence that the arrangement remained unchanged for decades.[1]

Why fifty elephants mattered

Elephants occur repeatedly in the accounts of Mahmud’s campaigns. They appear as defensive weapons, captured prizes, demanded tribute, and displays of royal wealth. At Narayan, their prominence ties the aftermath of the battle to the future military resources of the victor. An animal removed from one ruler’s service might become a resource in another ruler’s army.[1]

The chronicler describes the promised elephants as exceptionally large and strong. That qualification belongs to the rhetoric of a valuable gift. The stated fifty animals and two thousand men should remain attributed to him: they are reported terms, not figures checked against transport accounts. We also do not know from this passage the age, training, or eventual employment of each elephant.

Keeping an elephant required more than possession of the animal. Its practical value depended on handlers, feeding, movement, and continued care. The source does not itemise these arrangements. Its silence should prevent a fictional reconstruction of the caravan’s daily routine, but the omission also helps explain why an elephant tribute was a substantial demand. It transferred an expensive living resource rather than a symbolic token.

The promised soldiers had a different significance. Service at Mahmud’s court would draw manpower away from the tributary ruler and make some of it available to the conqueror. Al-Utbi does not explain whether the two thousand were to be replaced annually, how long they served, or what obligations their families retained at home. These questions remain open. The recorded demand is sufficient to demonstrate that submission reached beyond a payment of precious metal.

Peace for caravans

The account’s final sentence connects the settlement with secure caravans travelling between Khurasan and Hind. That is important evidence for the court’s presentation of the result. Mahmud’s war was made to lead to order; submission supposedly turned an unsafe passage into a protected commercial connection.[1]

This does not mean the merchants’ security compensated the people whose property had been taken or whose relatives had been killed. Different groups could experience the same political settlement very differently. A trader crossing a road after the agreement might benefit from reduced fighting, while a household in the attacked territory had already suffered the cost of obtaining that peace.

Nor does the brief statement establish the volume of trade, the products carried, or the exact road followed. Nazim interprets the expedition partly in terms of access toward the Ganges Doab, but that is his reconstruction. Al-Utbi’s direct claim is narrower: tribute was paid and caravans travelled securely. A modern account should not inflate it into a documented customs system or a complete commercial integration of northern India.[1][2]

The juxtaposition remains revealing. Military violence, religious prestige, material extraction, and caravan protection were not separate worlds. A ruler could destroy sacred objects during a raid, demand animals and men afterward, and then present the resulting security as a further achievement. That combination explains more of the source than a single motive assigned to every participant.

What changed, and what cannot be proved

The immediate outcome reported by al-Utbi is a successful raid followed by submission and deliveries. No sustained siege narrative survives in his passage. No local royal name is securely supplied. There is no evidence here that the whole of Rajasthan was conquered, that Delhi was the intended target, or that a battle at a precisely identified modern location determined the entire campaign.[1][2]

Narayan’s importance lies in a more specific development. Mahmud could turn the demonstrated threat of another attack into recurring obligations: elephants, manpower, gifts, and acknowledgement of superiority. The return to Ghazna did not necessarily end the relationship established through force. At the same time, the fragmentary evidence does not tell us how durable that relationship was after the first reported fulfilment.

The next dossier follows Mahmud’s renewed attack on Multan in 1010. That campaign targeted an Ismaili Muslim ruler and shows why these expeditions cannot be reduced to a single unchanging opposition between two religious populations. Return to the campaign guide to compare the dates, locations, and differing forms of submission.

Sources

  1. Al-Utbi, Tarikh-i Yamini, Arabic-derived extracts in H. M. Elliot and John Dowson, The History of India as Told by Its Own Historians, vol. II (1869), printed p. 36, “Capture of Narain” and “Embassy from India to Ghazna”; pp. 34–35 for the preceding Nagarkot display. Contemporary court narrative, with openly celebratory religious language. Read the original-source translation.
  2. Muhammad Nazim, The Life and Times of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazna (1931), printed pp. 101–103 and notes: dating, Narayanpur identification, the poetic reference, tribute, and commercial interpretation. This is a modern reconstruction; medieval works cited in its notes have not all been independently inspected here. Read the scholarly reconstruction.
  3. Elliot and Dowson, vol. II, Appendix, Note D, printed pp. 448–449: nineteenth-century discussion of Narayan’s location and the embassy. Its identifications are editorial proposals, not additional medieval testimony. Read the comparison.
  4. Al-Utbi, Kitab-i Yamini, James Reynolds’s 1858 translation from the Persian adaptation, chapter XXXI, printed pp. 360–362. Consult alongside the Arabic-derived extracts because headings and place spellings differ. Read Reynolds’s translation.

title: Multan, 1010: Mahmud’s return, Daud’s imprisonment, and persecution of the Ismailis
excerpt: The second Multan campaign ended with the removal of its Ismaili ruler and reported killings and imprisonment. Al-Biruni’s account of the city’s mosques reveals the religious politics behind this conquest of a Muslim principality.
html:
Mahmud’s campaign against Multan in 1010 was directed against a Muslim ruler and a Muslim religious community. Abu’l-Fath Daud, associated with the Ismaili principality of Multan, was taken prisoner and removed to a fortress outside India. The accompanying repression included killings and the distribution of prisoners among forts, according to the near-contemporary tradition cited by Muhammad Nazim. It is an episode in which political conquest and sectarian persecution were closely connected.[1]

The campaign belongs to the guide to Mahmud’s invasions. It followed the Narayan expedition of 1009, but it also resumed an older struggle: Mahmud had already attacked Multan in 1006. The return demonstrates that submission achieved during one expedition did not automatically produce lasting control.

Multan before the second attack

Multan occupied a strategic position in the river country of the northwest. Its political and commercial connections mattered to anyone moving between Ghazna, the Punjab, and the approaches to the Ganges plain. It was also a religious centre with a history older than the Ghaznavid campaigns. Al-Biruni’s account remembers a celebrated sun image, pilgrimage wealth, changes of rulers, and competing mosques within the same city.[2]

The rulers attacked by Mahmud were Ismaili Muslims. Sunni writers often described them with hostile terms, including the broad designation “Carmathians” or “Qarmatians.” Such vocabulary records the categories used by opponents. It should not be treated as a precise description of every resident’s beliefs or as a neutral verdict on the legitimacy of the community.

Mahmud’s own authority drew support from Sunni religious claims and recognition from the Abbasid caliphate. A rival Muslim principality could therefore be represented as a doctrinal enemy as well as a political obstacle. The first Multan campaign’s account explicitly joins accusations of religious error to disobedience. The two charges reinforced one another in the Ghaznavid presentation of intervention.[3]

This matters for the larger history of the invasions. A map coloured only by a Hindu–Muslim opposition would misdescribe the actors at Multan. It would also conceal the experience of Ismaili victims. Recognising their identity does not diminish violence against Hindu populations elsewhere; it makes the account of Mahmud’s wars more accurate.

Why Mahmud returned

The attack of 1006 had been followed by demands and arrangements for submission, but Mahmud was pulled back toward conflicts in his western dominions. Nazim explains the renewed expedition as the completion of a subjugation left unfinished when the threat of Ilak Khan required his departure. He dates the return to the beginning of 401 AH, approximately October 1010.[1]

That reconstruction cites Gardizi, a historian writing in the middle of the eleventh century. The Gardizi passages used here are accessed through Nazim’s citations and discussion, not through an independently checked translation of the entire Persian work. This distinction is important because the older Elliot and Dowson appendix gives the impression that the episode depends chiefly on much later chronicles. Gardizi’s evidence, as cited by Nazim, places a near-contemporary witness behind the reconstruction.[1][4]

Nazim suggests that Daud was probably creating renewed disturbance. The word “probably” deserves to survive. There is no surviving declaration from Daud in the sources inspected here explaining his intentions. A decision to resist imposed demands could appear as rebellion from Ghazna and as the preservation of local rule from Multan. The court’s political vocabulary does not settle that disagreement for us.

The history between the two expeditions also involved the appointment and revolt of Nawasa Shah, commonly identified with Sukhpal. His precise jurisdiction and relationship with neighbouring rulers are not entirely clear in the sources. That episode shows the difficulty of maintaining authority through appointed or subordinate rulers. It should not be used to invent a continuous, fully documented Ghaznavid provincial administration throughout the intervening years.[1][3]

What can be reconstructed of the campaign

The surviving evidence used here supports the return to Multan, the defeat or removal of its ruler, and harsh repression of his religious supporters. It does not supply a detailed contemporary siege diary. No secure day-by-day account survives in the inspected passages identifying each gate attacked, each defensive work, or the location of every confrontation.[1]

This limitation affects how the campaign should be pictured. Multan’s later fortifications, tombs, and gates are valuable records of the city’s long history, but they are not automatically the structures Daud defended. A modern photograph of the fort area cannot be used as architectural proof of the battlefield in 1010. The prominent tomb of Shah Rukn-e-Alam, for example, belongs to a much later period.

The absence of tactical detail does not make the consequences obscure. A ruler was captured, followers were reportedly killed or incarcerated, and religious authority within the city was reorganised. Those acts could transform the political life of Multan without leaving us a reliable account of the attack’s precise formation or duration.

The campaign should therefore be described as a successful coercive intervention, with the extent of permanent administrative control left open. “Conquest” can name the overthrow of a ruler, but it does not by itself prove that every outlying settlement was occupied continuously or that resistance had become impossible.

Daud’s capture and removal

Nazim’s account, citing Gardizi, says Abu’l-Fath Daud was taken prisoner and confined at Ghurak, also rendered Ghorak. Nazim locates the fortress roughly fifty miles northwest of Kandahar. The essential point is removal: the ruler of Multan was separated from the city and from the political resources on which his authority depended.[1]

The account says he remained there until his death. Nazim’s phrase that he ended his days in peace should not soften the condition into voluntary retirement. He was a prisoner. Even if the surviving source does not describe torture or execution, the loss of freedom and enforced residence were instruments of conquest.

Nor does the evidence permit a dramatic final speech, a detailed description of his cell, or a confidently dated death scene. Daud’s surviving historical role is largely filtered through the writers of the power that defeated him. Acknowledging that imbalance is more responsible than filling the gap with imagined dialogue.

His removal also changed the meaning of the earlier settlement. The first expedition had apparently allowed some accommodation with an existing ruler. The second brought an end to Daud’s ability to govern from Multan. Renewed force could thus replace a tributary arrangement with detention when the conqueror considered the arrangement inadequate or insecure.

Killings and imprisonment

Nazim reports, on Gardizi’s authority, that thousands of people whom the sources call Carmathians were killed or sent as prisoners to different forts. That is an explicit report of sectarian repression. It should be neither omitted behind a word such as “pacification” nor converted into a precisely verified population count.[1]

The categories in the report are broad. We do not have an individual register establishing how many victims were combatants, religious officials, townspeople, or dependants. The sources inspected here do not give a complete demographic profile. “Thousands,” where retained, must remain a chronicled claim rather than an audited total.

Distribution among forts would have separated prisoners from their local networks. That is a reasonable consequence of the reported action, although the text does not reveal each prisoner’s destination or subsequent life. It would be wrong to assert that every captive was executed, sold, or eventually released. The source supports detention and dispersal; it does not settle every individual fate.

This was violence within the history of Muslim societies as well as part of Mahmud’s invasions of India. The people targeted were not made less vulnerable by sharing Islam with their conqueror. Sectarian boundaries, political allegiance, and rival authority could override that common affiliation. Multan is therefore essential to an account of the campaigns that seeks to identify victims and motives accurately.

Al-Biruni and the two mosques

Al-Biruni supplies another kind of evidence. Writing around 1030, he describes changes in Multan’s religious buildings across several regimes. He says Jalam ibn Shaiban destroyed the old sun image and killed its priests when the Ismaili rulers established themselves. Those acts belong to an earlier phase in his narrative, not to Mahmud’s second expedition.[2]

This distinction prevents a serious error: the destruction of Multan’s famous sun image should not simply be assigned to Mahmud in 1010. Al-Biruni identifies a different agent. His description of the image as wooden and covered with red leather, with rubies for eyes, also differs from assumptions that every sacred object in these stories was a stone linga or an identical kind of statue.

The scholar then explains that Jalam closed the older mosque, which he associated with an earlier ruling tradition, and established worship in another building. When Mahmud overthrew the Ismaili rulers, the older mosque was restored to Friday worship and the second was allowed to decay. Al-Biruni says the latter site was being used for preparing bundles of henna in his own time.[2]

The passage ties religious authority to the use of urban space. Restoring one congregation’s mosque and abandoning another was a public alteration of legitimacy. It signalled which past was to be revived and which rival establishment was to lose status. This was more than a change of ruler’s name in a chronicle.

Al-Biruni does not date every architectural alteration to a particular day in the 1010 campaign. His evidence should therefore be used for the broader overthrow of the Ismaili regime and its institutional consequences. It corroborates a transformation of public worship without pretending to supply a complete account of the military operation.[2]

Did persecution end Ismaili power?

The campaign succeeded against Daud, but the later survival of opposition complicates any claim that Mahmud permanently extinguished the community. Nazim notes subsequent resistance associated with Daud’s son after the death of Mahmud’s successor Masud. The observation belongs to a later period, yet it is relevant to the limits of the 1010 outcome.[1]

Killing, captivity, and the replacement of rulers could suppress a political establishment without erasing religious identity. The reappearance of resistance does not reverse the suffering of those attacked in 1010. It demonstrates that violent success and lasting consent were different things.

The same distinction applies to the city itself. Multan continued to have a history after the invasion. Later monuments and institutions should not be presented as though the campaign reduced its entire future to a single catastrophe. A long-lived city could endure severe violence and remain a centre of settlement, commerce, and devotion under later powers.

The place of Multan in Mahmud’s wars

The second campaign reveals three connected uses of force: eliminating an unreliable political ruler, imposing a preferred religious establishment, and punishing a community represented as doctrinally hostile. Material advantage and the security of routes remained relevant, but the evidence does not permit religious repression to be dissolved into an exclusively economic explanation.

What can be stated firmly is that Daud was removed, captivity and killing formed part of the remembered suppression, and al-Biruni records a public reordering of the city’s mosques. The exact scale of the casualties and the full mechanics of provincial government remain less clear. Keeping these levels of certainty distinct allows the account to be both explicit and responsible.

Gardizi is consulted here through Nazim, not an independently inspected complete edition. Read Nazim’s reconstruction and citations.

title: Nandana, 1013–1014: winter, Shahi resistance, and the sale of captives
excerpt: A failed winter advance was followed by battle in the Salt Range, the loss of a Shahi fortress, and the enslavement of captives. Al-Utbi, Gardizi, and Kalhana preserve different parts of the campaign and its Kashmir connection.
html:
The expedition against Nandana was not an effortless advance through a defeated country. Mahmud’s first movement was checked by severe winter weather. The renewed attack encountered an entrenched defender, elephants blocking a narrow approach, and fighting that the court chronicler says lasted several days. The eventual Ghaznavid success brought the loss of a Shahi stronghold and a return march accompanied by people who had been enslaved.[1][2]

This article belongs to the guide to Mahmud’s invasions. It follows the second Multan campaign of 1010 and precedes the Thanesar expedition. Its destination, Nandana in the Salt Range, must not be confused with Narayan, attacked in 1009.

A Shahi position that still mattered

Earlier defeats had badly damaged Shahi power, but they had not ended all organised resistance. Muhammad Nazim reconstructs a surviving Shahi centre in the Salt Range after the Waihind and Nagarkot campaign. Anandapala was succeeded by his son Trilochanapala, whose family and allies continued to oppose Ghaznavid expansion.[2]

Nandana stood among the approaches through the Salt Range, in present-day Pakistan. Its importance came from the relationship between a defensible hill position and routes across the region. A stronghold could protect a ruler’s remaining authority, provide a refuge, and obstruct an opponent’s movement. Its military significance did not depend on controlling the entire subcontinent.

The sources use several forms of the name. Al-Utbi’s Arabic-derived account appears under Nardin in Elliot and Dowson; Gardizi and Baihaqi use forms closer to Nandana, according to Nazim. The names help explain why older campaign lists can look inconsistent. They do not justify merging this episode with the similarly named Narayan raid several years earlier.[1][2]

The Shahi side is also represented by varying names and titles. Al-Utbi’s Nidar Bhim is identified in modern reconstruction with Bhimapala, Trilochanapala’s son; the epithet is understood as “fearless.” Trilochanapala’s efforts to obtain assistance from Kashmir belong to the wider campaign. Father and son should not be compressed into a single person merely because the court account does not explain their dynasty for a modern reader.[2]

The winter movement of 1013

Al-Utbi dates Mahmud’s departure to late autumn in 404 AH. He describes snowfall so severe that the roads disappeared and passes were closed. Horses and camels suffered from the cold, and movement became uncertain. He then presents a pause in which supplies were assembled and commanders summoned before campaigning resumed in spring.[1]

Nazim reconstructs the first attempt as a departure around November 1013 followed by a return, then a renewed expedition around March 1014. His account uses the sequence in al-Utbi alongside other evidence. The distinction between a winter halt in the narrative and a reconstructed return to Ghazna is worth retaining: the inspected court text does not provide the same geographical precision at every stage.[1][2]

The weather is not incidental to the military history. An army needed passable roads, fodder, and transport before it could bring its strength to bear. Mahmud’s ability to win battles did not exempt his animals or supplies from mountain conditions. The pause also allowed time for preparation and reinforcement rather than simply suspending an unchanged column on the road.

Al-Utbi’s description is highly literary, including comparisons that turn the reassembled host into an almost immeasurable force. Those comparisons should not be converted into troop totals. The historical substance is that winter obstructed the movement and that the renewed expedition required organised resources.

Bhimapala closes the approach

In the reconstruction based on several sources, Trilochanapala entrusted the fort’s defence to Bhimapala while seeking support from Kashmir. Al-Utbi describes the defending commander occupying a narrow and difficult pass. Stones reinforced the position, and elephants blocked the approach.[1][2]

This arrangement used terrain to reduce the advantage of an attacker with substantial cavalry. A constricted approach limited how many mounted men could fight at once. Elephants added a formidable obstacle, while hills and prepared works offered protection to the men behind them. The account presents a deliberate defensive choice, not a population waiting passively to be attacked.

Mahmud distributed commands among several officers. Al-Utbi names Amir Nasr, Arslan al-Jazib, Abu Abdallah al-Tai, and Altuntash in the wings, advance, and centre. His descriptions praise their strength and courage, but the named arrangement also suggests differentiated bodies under recognisable leadership rather than one undirected mass.[1]

The composition of the attacking force was varied. The chronicler mentions Daylamite troops and Afghan spearmen in the attack on the difficult position. Such details matter because a simple picture of an exclusively mounted Turkish army obscures the infantry and regional forces needed for fighting in confined ground.[1]

Several days of fighting

Al-Utbi says the struggle continued for several days. Some defenders were drawn out into the plain, where Ghaznavid cavalry attacked them. After reinforcements arrived, the defending commander brought out a larger force, with the hills behind it and elephants on the wings. The narrative thus records a change from a protected position to a more open engagement.[1]

It would be easy to turn that movement into a confident claim that Bhimapala made an obvious blunder. The sources do not preserve his own assessment. Reinforcements, pressure on supplies, the position of neighbouring forces, or an opportunity perceived on the ground could all affect such a decision, but none should be invented as his documented reason. What survives is the opponent’s account of the movement and its result.

When the elephants advanced, al-Utbi says the attackers directed arrows against their eyes and trunks. The description makes their vulnerability explicit without proving that every elephant reacted identically. The source’s concluding celebration of captured animals confirms their value to the victor, but it provides no independently checked tally for this campaign.[1]

The same passage records serious injury to Abu Abdallah al-Tai. Mahmud sent guards to bring the wounded commander out of the fighting and ordered him placed on an elephant. The episode serves the chronicler’s praise of courage and royal concern, yet it also acknowledges that victory did not mean an absence of danger or wounds among the attacking leadership.[1]

The defenders were defeated. Al-Utbi describes killing in hills, ravines, and watercourses, as well as the seizure of elephants and other property. There is no reliable overall death toll. The violence can be stated plainly without adding a number the source does not provide.

The fortress and the Kashmir connection

Al-Utbi’s account concentrates on the battle, booty, and religious significance of victory. Nazim supplements it with Gardizi’s account of the siege of Nandana: mining beneath the walls, archery against the defenders, and surrender by a garrison that could not maintain resistance. These details are Gardizi’s as transmitted through Nazim’s reconstruction, not additional sentences supplied by al-Utbi.[2]

The fall of the fort did not end the broader operation. Trilochanapala had sought assistance from Sangramaraja of Kashmir. A force under Tunga came to his aid. Kalhana’s Rajatarangini, written in the twelfth century, preserves a Kashmir-side account that is valuable because it comes from a different historical tradition, although it too was composed after the events.[2][3]

Kalhana describes initial success by the Kashmir commander followed by defeat when the invading leader attacked more effectively. The passage criticises Tunga’s judgment and gives Trilochanapala a separate role in continued resistance. It should not be reduced to the Ghaznavid court’s claim that divine favour made victory automatic. The accounts share an outcome while arranging blame and courage differently.[2][3]

The precise relationship between each engagement and each valley needs caution. Nazim places the subsequent confrontation north of the Jhelum and combines the Persian and Kashmir narratives. That synthesis helps explain the campaign, but a modern map should not imply that every battlefield coordinate is secure.

The captives on the return march

The most disturbing passage in al-Utbi comes after the victory. He says captives became so numerous that their price fell, and that people who had held respected positions at home were reduced to slavery under ordinary shopkeepers. He welcomes this humiliation as an expression of religious triumph.[1]

This is evidence of enslavement, not merely a euphemistic transfer of “booty.” The people taken were deprived of freedom and made available for purchase. The chronicler’s interest in the collapse of status tells us something about his values: degradation that a reader may recognise as suffering becomes a reason for celebration in the victor’s narrative.

The passage does not provide a reliable total or name individual victims. It does not identify the occupation, age, or destination of every captive. Those limits should prevent an invented demographic reconstruction, but they do not weaken the direct evidence that the taking and cheap sale of human beings formed part of the reported outcome.

It also shows how warfare reached beyond the battlefield. Captivity could follow the army into markets and households far from the attacked region. A victory’s consequences were therefore not exhausted when the last formation withdrew from the pass. The forced movement of people was part of the material return from campaigning.

The temple inscription and a translation error

Al-Utbi includes a story about an inscription found at a temple. In the Elliot and Dowson translation, it claimed an antiquity of fifty thousand years. The chronicler contrasts this with the much shorter sacred chronology accepted by Mahmud’s advisers, who reject the stone’s testimony.[1]

The story is evidence for a dispute over religious history as represented at the Ghaznavid court. It is not proof that the temple was fifty thousand years old. Nor can the inscription now be treated as an independently verified archaeological document simply because a chronicler reports it. Nazim’s discussion even gives a different enormous figure when paraphrasing the episode, another reason not to use the number as established dating.[2]

There is a further problem in the old English wording. Elliot and Dowson render the temple’s sacred object as the “great Budda.” Nazim points out that the underlying word budd, related to Persian but, means an idol in this context. That wording does not establish that the temple was Buddhist.[2]

The correction has real consequences. A mistaken translation can create an entire religious identification that then travels through later summaries. The responsible description is a temple and sacred image reported in al-Utbi’s narrative, with no confident Buddhist attribution based on this phrase alone.

A stronghold lost, resistance displaced

Gardizi’s evidence, as cited by Nazim, supplies the appointment of a Ghaznavid officer at Nandana and a return in the summer of 1014. This distinguishes the outcome from a raid that simply removed portable treasure and departed. A garrison or appointed custodian could make the site part of a continuing structure of military control.[2]

Trilochanapala nevertheless survived and continued to appear in the politics of northern India. Nazim reconstructs his movement toward the eastern Punjab and the foothills. A lost fortress and a defeated army did not mean that every Shahi alliance or family member vanished. Subsequent campaigns encountered rulers and relationships reshaped by these earlier defeats.

Nandana’s conquest therefore combined a military breakthrough with a human catastrophe: defensive positions were overcome, a fortress was lost, and captives were sold. At the same time, winter resistance, the duration of the fighting, and the appeal to Kashmir show the limits and challenges faced by the invading force. This is a more substantial history than a simple entry declaring another effortless victory.

Continue with the attack on Thanesar in 1014–1015, or return to the campaign guide to compare the evidence for the separate expeditions.

Sources

  1. Al-Utbi, Tarikh-i Yamini, Arabic-derived extracts in H. M. Elliot and John Dowson, The History of India as Told by Its Own Historians, vol. II (1869), printed pp. 37–39, “Conquest of Nardin”: winter obstruction, formations, fighting, the inscription, and enslavement. Its devotional language and reported figures belong to a court panegyric. Read the original-source translation.
  2. Muhammad Nazim, The Life and Times of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazna (1931), printed pp. 91–94 and notes: dates, Nandana identification, Bhimapala and Trilochanapala, Gardizi’s siege narrative, the Kashmir alliance, garrison, and the correction of “Budda.” Gardizi’s passages are used here through this reconstruction. Read Nazim and his medieval-source citations.
  3. Kalhana, Rajatarangini, book VII, verses 47–69, discussed and cited by Nazim, pp. 91–93. Twelfth-century Kashmir narrative, not an eyewitness account; used here through Nazim’s checked references rather than an independently inspected complete edition. Consult the source discussion.
  4. Al-Utbi, Kitab-i Yamini, James Reynolds’s translation from the Persian adaptation (1858), chapter XXXVII, printed pp. 388–393. Compare with the Arabic-derived extract because this version’s heading and dating differ. Read the parallel nineteenth-century translation.

title: Thanesar, 1014–1015: the river battle and the removal of Cakrasvamin
excerpt: Al-Utbi describes a contested river crossing, captured elephants, and plunder. Al-Biruni supplies a sharper material consequence: Thanesar’s bronze Cakrasvamin lay at Ghazna, removed from the city that venerated it.
html:
The most tangible consequence of Mahmud’s attack on Thanesar appears in al-Biruni’s description of a displaced sacred image. The bronze Cakrasvamin, nearly the size of a person, had been removed from the city that venerated it and lay in the hippodrome at Ghazna. It was there alongside the sacred object later taken from Somnath. The scholar’s account gives the campaign a material aftermath beyond a list of victories: a religious object had become a public sign of its worshippers’ defeat.[1]

Al-Utbi supplies a different part of the story: an army crossing difficult country, a defended river, hard fighting, captured elephants, and plunder. Read together, the accounts reveal military extraction and deliberate religious humiliation. They also require care over the date and the relationship between the battle on the approach and the seizure of the town.[1][2]

This dossier belongs to the guide to Mahmud’s invasions. It follows the Nandana campaign of 1013–1014 in the reconstruction used here. The next article examines the failed first attempt to enter Kashmir in 1015–1016.

Thanesar as a sacred destination

Thanesar, in present-day Haryana, had a religious importance that the near-contemporary sources explicitly acknowledge. Al-Biruni says Hindus held the city in high veneration and identifies its famous image as Cakrasvamin, explaining the name through the cakra, or discus. His description preserves information about the object’s material, size, and religious meaning.[1]

This was not simply a treasury that happened to contain metal. A sacred image could connect worshippers to a place, a ritual tradition, and remembered history. Taking it away therefore damaged an institution’s devotional life as well as transferring a valuable object. The public destination at Ghazna further changed its meaning: an object of honour at home became a trophy in the conqueror’s capital.

Al-Biruni also reports a traditional association with Bharata and ancient wars. That is evidence of the origin story attached to the image, not an independently established date for casting the bronze. A modern account can preserve the tradition without treating sacred chronology as a metallurgical examination.

No photograph of Thanesar’s present religious buildings should be described as an image of Cakrasvamin in its original eleventh-century setting. The text identifies the removed bronze; it does not identify a surviving modern shrine as the same building Mahmud encountered. Modern landscapes help locate a historical city, but they cannot replace the missing object and its original context.

A date with competing traditions

This article uses 1014–1015, the sequence reconstructed by Muhammad Nazim: departure in autumn 405 AH, approximately October 1014, and return in the following spring. The position after Nandana agrees with al-Utbi’s order, while Nazim cites Ibn al-Athir for the year.[3]

The sources do not all agree. Nazim’s note explicitly says Gardizi places the expedition in 402 AH, corresponding to 1011–1012. Other traditional lists use an earlier date. The disagreement should remain visible rather than disappearing behind an apparently exact calendar entry. Gardizi’s earlier date is especially important because he is near-contemporary; the later dating cannot simply be described as his own statement.[3]

Al-Utbi’s surviving extract provides a narrative but no explicit year for this operation. It is consequently stronger evidence for the reported fighting than for a modern departure day. The use of a two-year title also reflects a campaigning season extending across autumn and spring, rather than the assumption that an Islamic lunar year and a Common Era year share the same boundaries.

These uncertainties do not make the attack imaginary. The displacement of Cakrasvamin is independently reported by al-Biruni. They affect the calendar and the arrangement of the episode within a reconstructed series, not the existence of every action described in it.

Elephants and religious purpose

Al-Utbi begins with Mahmud learning that the country possessed elephants especially valued for warfare. The chronicler connects the ruler’s possession of them with resistance and then declares the invasion a campaign against idolatry. The passage gives material acquisition and religious purpose together.[2]

The elephants were military resources. Their seizure could weaken one ruler and strengthen another, and their capture was repeatedly counted among Mahmud’s achievements. The source’s claim about a particular breed should remain attributed to it; it does not give a surviving veterinary or breeding record that would establish the animals’ precise origin.

The religious purpose is equally explicit in the narrative. It should not be omitted on the assumption that every declaration of faith concealed an exclusively financial motive. Conversely, a writer’s devotional explanation does not erase the tangible value of animals, wealth, and political submission. These purposes could operate together without being identical.

Nazim also describes an offer attributed to Trilochanapala to deliver fifty elephants if Thanesar were spared. The proposed bargain belongs to the wider source tradition he reconstructs. It illustrates a possible attempt to exchange material resources for the safety of a venerated place; it is not a surviving treaty whose terms can be independently examined.[3]

The approach and the defended river

Al-Utbi says the army crossed barren country with little or no water before reaching a river passing through difficult ground. The claim that no person had previously traversed the desert belongs to the chronicler’s celebration of an unprecedented achievement. It should not be turned into a literal assertion that the landscape had never supported travellers.[2]

At the river, defenders occupied a protected position behind elephants, with infantry and cavalry. The banks were steep and the bottom stony. The important military point is the combination of water, terrain, and a prepared opposing force. A crossing army would have to negotiate the obstacle before it could deploy all its strength effectively.

The river is not named in the passage. Nazim identifies it with the Sutlej near its emergence from the hills and associates the defending ruler with a figure called Ram in Gardizi. He also discusses possible identifications of the ruler’s territory. These are reconstruction steps; the Arabic-derived extract does not itself label the site with a modern bridge or town.[2][3]

It is therefore safer to call this the river battle on the approach to Thanesar than to picture it automatically at the edge of the city. The expedition could include a major engagement some distance from its eventual sacred destination. Separating those stages prevents an attractive but unsupported single-scene narrative.

How the crossing was forced

According to al-Utbi, Mahmud sent troops across at two different fords to attack both sides of the defending position. Another force moved along the riverbank against men concentrated in the ravines. The tactic sought to make the defenders confront pressure from several directions rather than relying on a single frontal crossing.[2]

The battle continued into the evening. The chronicler reports that the defenders eventually fled, abandoning elephants that were driven into Mahmud’s camp. One escaped capture, while the largest were reserved for the ruler. This is a specific account of spoils divided after a hard engagement, even though the text does not supply a dependable complete tally.

Al-Utbi describes the water as discoloured by blood and no longer drinkable. Such imagery makes the killing explicit, but it is also a common literary way to magnify victory. It is not an independent environmental measurement from which casualties can be calculated. The account supports severe fighting and deaths, not a scientifically recoverable volume of blood.

The source says darkness limited the pursuit. That detail places a practical boundary on the victor’s opportunity to kill. The author regrets an interruption that a modern reader may recognise as permitting some people to escape. His emotional alignment with the invading army must remain apparent when the incident is retold.

Nazim’s reconstruction also says the attackers’ losses were heavier than those of the defenders, citing al-Utbi and Gardizi. That assessment should remain attributed to the reconstruction, because the inspected extract gives no complete figures on either side. It nevertheless cautions against equating eventual possession of the field with an inexpensive victory. An army could capture the opponent’s elephants and still pay heavily in casualties; the surviving celebration of booty should not make its own losses disappear.[3]

Plunder and removal from Thanesar

Nazim’s reconstruction distinguishes the river victory from the entry into Thanesar. It says the city’s ruler fled and that Mahmud entered without another battle, plundered the place, and removed Cakrasvamin. For this stage Nazim uses Gardizi and al-Biruni rather than pretending that al-Utbi supplies every detail.[3]

That distinction changes the account of violence. A hard-fought approach does not establish that the city itself underwent an equally prolonged siege. Nor does entry without opposition imply a harmless occupation. Property could be seized and a sacred institution attacked even where an organised garrison did not contest the gate.

Al-Biruni’s independent description is particularly valuable here. He identifies the bronze by name and material and places it at Ghazna. His work was completed around 1030, close enough to the campaigns to provide a stronger chronological anchor than the colourful stories written several centuries later.[1]

The scholar does not claim to have stood beside Mahmud during the assault. His evidence concerns the object and its remembered origin, not a complete eyewitness itinerary. Its strength should be used precisely: it confirms a displaced sacred bronze and the connection to Thanesar, while leaving other battlefield details to other accounts.

What a public trophy accomplished

Transporting a revered object to a distant capital served more than the acquisition of metal. The image could be displayed where the victor’s subjects, soldiers, visitors, and rivals encountered it. Its presence made an otherwise distant campaign visible within Ghazna’s public space.[1]

Al-Biruni later places the Somnath object beside it. The juxtaposition suggests how separate campaigns could be assembled into a cumulative royal statement. Religious objects from different regions were removed from their communities and brought into a setting controlled by the same ruler. Their shared destination linked victories that had occurred years apart.

This should not be confused with museum preservation. An object displayed as the evidence of another community’s humiliation has a different purpose from an object retained for historical understanding. The point of the removal in these accounts was bound to conquest and the degradation of a rival religious authority.

The bronze’s later fate is not securely supplied in the inspected passages. Its location around al-Biruni’s time does not establish an unbroken chain of custody to a present collection. An image of a different bronze cannot responsibly be labelled as this captured Cakrasvamin merely because its general iconography resembles the description.

Consequences and limits

The reported outcomes were military defeat on the approach, captured elephants, plunder, and the removal of a major sacred object. The evidence is explicit enough to resist euphemism, but it does not supply a reliable overall death toll, a complete list of destroyed buildings, or a detailed record of permanent Ghaznavid administration in Thanesar.[1][2][3]

Nor did this expedition mean every remaining objective could be reached. The subsequent Kashmir campaign encountered a different relationship of fortifications, mountain routes, and winter conditions. An army successful against one river position could still fail before another kind of obstacle.

Thanesar’s history in this series rests on that combination: a forceful military narrative and an unusually specific record of cultural dispossession. Continue with the first Kashmir attempt of 1015–1016, or return to the campaign guide.

Sources

  1. Al-Biruni, India, translated by Eduard C. Sachau, vol. I, chapter XI, printed p. 117: Thanesar’s religious importance, the bronze Cakrasvamin, its approximate size, and its presence in Ghazna’s hippodrome with the Somnath object. Read the digitised near-contemporary source. See also vol. II, chapter LVIII, printed p. 103, parallel reference to the transported objects.
  2. Al-Utbi, Tarikh-i Yamini, extracts in H. M. Elliot and John Dowson, The History of India as Told by Its Own Historians, vol. II (1869), printed pp. 39–41, “Conquest of Tanesar”: elephants, declared religious purpose, the river battle, deaths, and booty. The blood-filled-stream description is the chronicler’s rhetoric. Read the original-source translation.
  3. Muhammad Nazim, The Life and Times of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazna (1931), printed pp. 103–104 and notes: 405 AH reconstruction, Gardizi’s conflicting 402 AH date, the proposed Sutlej identification, and the distinction between river battle and entry into Thanesar. Gardizi is accessed here through Nazim. Read the scholarly reconstruction and source notes.
  4. Al-Utbi, Kitab-i Yamini, translated from the Persian adaptation by James Reynolds (1858), chapter XXXVIII, printed pp. 393–395. Read the parallel version.

title: Kashmir, 1015–1016: the fortress Mahmud failed to take
excerpt: At Lohkot, mountain defences and winter conditions stopped Mahmud’s first attempt to enter Kashmir. The sources record a failed siege, a dangerous retreat, and the survival of a region beyond his effective reach.
html:
Mahmud did not conquer Kashmir. In the expedition conventionally dated 1015–1016, his advance was stopped before a mountain fortress called Lohkot. The siege failed, winter disrupted his communications, and the army withdrew. Later accounts add a dangerous return through water-covered ground in which men died. This episode is essential to the history of his invasions because it records a defended limit to his power rather than another successful raid.[1][2]

It belongs to the guide to Mahmud’s invasions and follows the Thanesar expedition in the chronology adopted here. Kashmir had already entered the story through assistance offered to Shahi resistance during the Nandana campaign. The failed attempt should remain separate from the second Kashmir and Lahore sequence of 1021–1022.

The political connection with the Shahis

Kashmir was not an isolated landscape outside the politics of the Punjab. Its ruler, Sangramaraja, had supported Trilochanapala against Mahmud. A Kashmir force under Tunga appears in the accounts of the fighting associated with the loss of Nandana. The connection placed the Kashmir court within the network of powers resisting Ghaznavid expansion.[1]

Muhammad Nazim suggests that Mahmud’s subsequent advance was probably intended to punish Sangramaraja for that assistance. The explanation is plausible, but its status matters: it is a historian’s reconstruction, not a surviving declaration by Mahmud specifying the purpose of the expedition. Strategic access, the subordination of a neighbouring power, and the continuation of earlier conflict could all have mattered without leaving us a ranked list of motives.[1]

The previous conflict also helps explain why a mountain approach mattered. Defeating a Shahi force in one region did not eliminate the possibility of refuge, assistance, or renewed alliances elsewhere. Control could remain incomplete as long as a neighbouring court retained the ability to offer support beyond the reach of a particular victory.

None of this establishes a unified command joining every opponent of Mahmud. Kashmir had its own ruler, interests, and military decisions. The Shahis had theirs. Their cooperation should be described as an alliance or intervention supported by the sources, without turning several courts into a single modern nation-state.

Lohkot and the mountain approach

The fortress’s name appears as Lohkot, Loharkotta, and related forms. Nazim, drawing on Gardizi and Aurel Stein’s interpretation of Kashmir geography, identifies it with Loharin. He reconstructs an advance through the Jhelum region and the valley of the Tohi toward the approaches to the Tosa Maidan pass.[1]

This geography should be presented as a reconstruction. The nineteenth-century Elliot and Dowson appendix proposed a different identification and openly called the location difficult to fix. Their uncertainty cannot be erased by adopting whichever fort in a modern photograph looks most dramatic. A precise label needs a defensible relationship to the textual and topographical evidence.[2]

What is more secure than every coordinate is the military relationship: a fortified position obstructed passage toward Kashmir. Mahmud could not obtain his objective merely by winning a battle on an open plain. He had to get past a place whose garrison and terrain restricted his movement.

That is the practical significance of a mountain fortress. An army passing through a narrow corridor might leave a hostile stronghold behind it only at substantial risk to movement and supply. The sources do not preserve Mahmud’s full operational assessment, but the decision to besiege Lohkot indicates that he could not treat it as irrelevant.

What survives of the siege

Nazim dates the expedition to 406 AH, beginning in 1015 and ending with a return in spring 1016. For the siege he cites Gardizi, a near-contemporary historian. The Gardizi material here is consulted through Nazim’s references and discussion; an independently inspected complete English translation has not been used.[1]

The reconstruction says the fort had a reputation for being exceptionally difficult to take. Mahmud invested it, but about a month of effort did not produce a successful capture. Heavy snow then cut his communications, and he raised the siege. This is the central sequence supported by the evidence: attempt, resistance, deteriorating conditions, withdrawal.[1]

The later Firishta narrative, quoted in Elliot and Dowson, similarly emphasises the fort’s height and strength, increasing cold, snowfall, and reinforcements reaching the defenders from Kashmir. Firishta wrote in the early seventeenth century, around six centuries after the campaign. His version may preserve older material, but it should not be given the authority of a correspondent watching the siege.[2]

No inspected source supplies a complete engineering account. We do not know the dimensions of the assault works, the daily expenditure of arrows, or the number of defenders on each wall. Statements that a particular tower was mined or that a named gate was stormed would therefore exceed the evidence. The failure itself is sufficiently consequential without imaginary siege choreography.

Why snow could change the outcome

Winter affected the campaign through movement and communication. A mountain army depended on routes for supplies, messages, reinforcement, and eventual withdrawal. Snow that obstructed those routes could make continued presence more dangerous even if the besieging force remained formidable in a direct encounter.[1]

The issue was not simply whether individual soldiers could endure cold. Horses and transport animals needed food and passable ground. An army carrying weapons, baggage, and provisions had different requirements from a small group travelling on foot. The sources do not provide a full supply inventory, so those requirements should be explained as general constraints rather than reconstructed as a fictional daily ration schedule.

The defenders also had an advantage that cannot be reduced to weather. They held the position Mahmud needed to overcome. In Firishta’s later narrative, reinforcements came from Kashmir while the attackers’ situation worsened. Terrain, a functioning garrison, and support from the interior combined to make time work against the besieger.[2]

It would be misleading to say snow alone “defeated” an otherwise uncontested army. The army remained outside a fort that had resisted its efforts. Weather made that unresolved military problem more costly and eventually untenable. The outcome belonged to both the effectiveness of the defended position and the conditions surrounding it.

Retreat and the water-covered plain

Nazim’s reconstruction adds a dangerous return: Mahmud lost his way in the hills and reached ground covered with water. Troops died, and the ruler escaped with difficulty. Nazim cites later authors, including Ibn al-Athir, for this portion; he uses Gardizi for the subsequent wintering and return to Ghazna.[1]

Firishta’s account in Elliot and Dowson offers a similarly alarming picture of water in every direction and an army unable to extricate itself for several days. Its dramatic language should remain attributed. The inspected evidence does not permit an exact reconstruction of the flooded area, the number drowned, or the day on which each body of men escaped.[2]

Older editors tried to identify the water with specific rivers and plains. Nazim proposes another topographical possibility in a note. Those suggestions are useful research leads, not a licence to draw one certain retreat line on a modern map. The source tradition supports serious difficulty involving water; the exact location remains less secure.

This episode also requires a distinction between battlefield killing and deaths during withdrawal. The sources do not establish that every man lost was slain by Kashmir troops. Some may have died through conditions on the route as the narratives describe. Equally, describing the losses as environmental does not turn the failed invasion into an event without military responsibility or strategic consequences.

Winter in the Punjab

According to Gardizi as used by Nazim, Mahmud spent the remaining winter months in the Punjab before returning to Ghazna in spring, approximately March 1016. The campaign therefore did not end in an immediate uninterrupted ride from the failed siege to the capital.[1]

Wintering away from Ghazna placed demands on the army and on the territory supporting it. The inspected passage does not itemise requisitions or name households affected by its presence. It would be wrong to invent a specific plunder operation for every place where the force paused. The narrower conclusion is that withdrawal from Lohkot still required a prolonged management of troops beyond the principal objective.

The distinction also helps explain the campaign’s two-year date. An expedition launched in 1015 could continue into 1016 through retreat and winter quarters. A list that assigns each campaign a single year may obscure this duration and make separate stages appear to be separate invasions.

A gap in the victory chronicle

Al-Utbi does not supply a continuous account of this failed siege. His history celebrates Mahmud’s successes and gives only indirect material relevant to Kashmir in this part of the sequence. Elliot and Dowson noticed the omission but relied heavily on much later authors when discussing the expedition.[2]

The near-contemporary Gardizi evidence cited by Nazim improves that older picture. It means the first Kashmir attempt should not be dismissed as a story recorded only six centuries later. At the same time, Gardizi’s testimony should not be silently merged with every detail supplied by Firishta. Their different dates and distances from the event remain important to the strength of individual claims.[1][2]

The sources also disagree over the year: the Tabaqat-i Akbari places the attempt in 407 AH, while the reconstruction used here follows 406 AH. This is one reason an apparently tidy seventeen-campaign calendar cannot be treated as an enumeration delivered intact by a single contemporary author. The campaign’s failed outcome is clearer than every detail of its modern numbering.

Kashmir beyond Mahmud’s reach

Al-Biruni’s broader account of the effects of Mahmud’s wars includes an important observation. He says learning had retreated from conquered regions to places beyond the conquerors’ reach, including Kashmir and Benares. His description is a retrospective judgment about displacement and intellectual life, not a census of every scholar who moved.[3]

The statement nevertheless fits the central limit illustrated here: Kashmir remained outside Mahmud’s successful conquest. It could shelter institutions and connections that were not easily absorbed by victory elsewhere. That survival did not mean the region was untouched by surrounding conflict; the alliance with the Shahis and the siege at its approaches show otherwise.

Al-Biruni’s wording should not be expanded into a claim that all learning disappeared from every conquered place or that every scholar migrated to Kashmir. He names destinations and describes a disruptive process; he does not enumerate institutions or people. The important relationship is between the security of a region beyond the army’s reach and the possibility of maintaining intellectual life there. Its scale cannot be calculated from this passage alone.[3]

The failure also did not permanently end Mahmud’s ambitions. He attempted the Kashmir approach again in the sequence dated 1021–1022, with another unsuccessful siege. The later attempt should be studied on its own evidence rather than used to erase the earlier one as an accidental duplication.[1]

The first expedition therefore changes the shape of the series. Mahmud’s forces could inflict severe destruction and carry away wealth and people, but their power had geographical, logistical, and military limits. At Lohkot, those limits were defended successfully.

Continue with the much larger Mathura and Kannauj expedition of 1018–1019, or return to the campaign guide.

See pp. 91–93 for Kashmir’s intervention in the preceding Shahi conflict. Gardizi and the Kashmir topographical identifications are accessed here through Nazim’s reconstruction.
