title: Mathura and Kannauj, 1018–1019: temples burned, cities plundered, people enslaved
excerpt: Al-Utbi’s near-contemporary narrative records coercive submission, killings, the burning of Mathura’s temples, plunder at Kannauj, and the sale of captives across the Ghaznavid world. Its detail demands an equally careful account of names, dates, and exaggerated totals.
html:
In the winter of 1018–1019, Mahmud’s army crossed into the Ganges–Yamuna region and attacked a succession of political and religious centres. The campaign was not one battle. It included submission under threat at Baran, a deadly engagement with Kulchand, the plunder and burning of temples at Mathura, the seizure of Kannauj’s fortifications, attacks on other strongholds, and a pursuit ending in killing and captivity at Sharwa. The return brought prisoners into markets extending far beyond northern India.[1]

Al-Utbi’s near-contemporary account is unusually explicit. It describes admiration for Mathura’s architecture followed by an order to burn and level the temples. It also describes captives sold cheaply and dispersed to Khurasan, Iraq, and Transoxiana. These are the court chronicler’s own claims, made in celebration rather than condemnation. They provide evidence of violence and enslavement while requiring caution over enormous numbers and triumphant religious language.[1]

This account forms part of the guide to Mahmud’s invasions. It follows the failed first Kashmir attempt of 1015–1016 and leads to the renewed eastern and Chandela campaigning. The series keeps these episodes separate for reading without claiming that every boundary in the traditional invasion lists is equally secure.

Preparing an eastern expedition

Al-Utbi begins with preparation after Mahmud’s return from Khwarazm. Spies were sent toward the Indian frontier, horses and troops were allowed time to recover, and a further campaign was planned. This opening matters: the expedition was not simply an improvised pursuit from the previous battlefield. Intelligence, rest, and a decision about the next objective preceded movement.[1]

The chronicler says volunteers from Transoxiana and neighbouring regions wanted service in a religious war. His reported twenty thousand is not an audited muster total. What the passage establishes more securely is the way a distant campaign could be represented as an opportunity for religious merit as well as military reward. The army’s participants were recruited into a framework that celebrated conquest and the defeat of rival worship.

Al-Utbi also makes extravagant claims about the extent of earlier conquest. They should not be adopted as a literal map of Ghaznavid government. Mahmud had not brought the entire subcontinent under continuous administration; the failure in Kashmir alone demonstrates a limit. Military reach, tributary agreements, garrisons, and direct rule were different forms of power.

The approaching campaign would extend that reach toward major river cities. Mathura and Kannauj were not interchangeable targets. Their political and religious histories differed, as did the circumstances of the army’s arrival. The narrative joins them through the itinerary of the invading force, not because their inhabitants formed a single army or polity.

Crossing the rivers

The route required repeated crossings of the Punjab rivers before the army reached the Yamuna. Al-Utbi names the Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, and Sutlej in forms transmitted through Arabic and Persian. He emphasises their depth and the danger posed to horses and baggage animals.[1]

The chronicler dates the Yamuna crossing to 20 Rajab 409 AH, rendered in the edition as 2 December 1018. The date is one of the campaign’s stronger chronological anchors. It is more useful than an attempt to derive a precise departure day from a later writer’s general reference to spring or the campaigning season.[1][2]

Local rulers and guides appear in the account. One figure associated with routes toward Kashmir offers submission and guidance. That detail shows how an invading army could use regional knowledge rather than advance wholly independently of local political choices. It does not prove universal voluntary cooperation by the people of every territory crossed.

The source’s marching descriptions also emphasise distance, early movement, and difficult terrain. We should preserve the logistical importance without turning the prose into an invented travel diary. The inspected evidence does not establish a modern road for every stage or the exact place where each river was crossed.

Baran: submission under the sword

At Baran, al-Utbi names a ruler called Hardat. The chronicle says he feared for his life as Mahmud approached and concluded that conversion to Islam offered the safest course. It then reports his appearance with ten thousand men declaring acceptance of the religion.[1]

The numerical claim requires attribution. We do not have a register of ten thousand individuals or evidence allowing us to reconstruct each person’s belief. But the source’s explanation of the ruler’s fear makes coercion integral to the episode. A profession of faith made when military punishment threatens is not evidence of an entirely unpressured religious decision.

The account celebrates this outcome as divine assistance to Mahmud. A modern narrative need not share that evaluation to report the event. It can say plainly that the court writer depicts threatened violence producing submission and conversion, while leaving the long-term religious lives of the people concerned unresolved.

Baran also demonstrates an alternative to immediate battle. A local ruler could try to avoid attack through compliance. That choice might preserve lives in the short term while demanding political and religious concessions. The source leaves no basis for assuming that every ruler faced identical conditions or that submission guaranteed the same treatment everywhere.

Kulchand’s resistance and death

The next major engagement in al-Utbi’s narrative concerns Kulchand. The source presents him as a powerful ruler with wealth, elephants, strong fortifications, and troops. His position was associated with forest and a nearby river. The name and site have been identified in different ways by later historians; an exact modern battlefield should not be asserted without further evidence.[1][2]

Mahmud’s advance guard forced its way through the wooded approach. Fighting followed with close use of swords and spears. When the defenders could no longer hold, some attempted escape across the river. Al-Utbi reports people killed, captured, or drowned during this flight.[1]

He claims nearly fifty thousand killed or drowned. That is a court chronicler’s total, not an independently checked casualty count. The enormity of the figure should not become the foundation for a precise demographic calculation. The reported forms of harm—battle deaths, killing during flight, drowning, and captivity—are substantial even when the total remains uncertain.

The same source says Kulchand killed his wife and then himself with a dagger. The account should not romanticise her death as a chosen sacrifice: the text does not preserve her consent or perspective. Nor can a single reported act be made evidence for a universal practice among every community attacked by Mahmud. It is a particular violent ending recorded by an enemy chronicler.[1]

Al-Utbi claims 185 elephants were taken. As elsewhere, these were material prizes as well as signs of victory. A defending ruler’s loss of them could affect his remaining military capacity, while their transfer advertised the invader’s success. The number belongs to the source and should remain attached to it.

Mathura’s architecture in the conqueror’s account

Mathura receives a striking description. Al-Utbi presents a river city with strong stone walls, gates built on substantial foundations, numerous masonry religious buildings, iron fastenings, and wooden structural supports. At its centre stood a temple he regarded as beyond adequate description.[1]

He then gives the substance of a letter attributed to Mahmud praising the extraordinary cost and time that would be required to reproduce the central building. Its enormous valuation and two-hundred-year construction estimate belong to admiration expressed through hyperbole. They cannot be treated as a surviving contractor’s budget or an exact archaeological chronology.

The admiration is nevertheless significant. The narrative does not portray the buildings as worthless or artistically negligible. Their destruction followed an acknowledgement of exceptional workmanship. Cultural achievement and vulnerability to attack were thus visible in the same account.

The description also links architectural splendour to sacred objects and precious materials. Al-Utbi lists gold and silver images, rubies, a sapphire, and impressive metal weights. Those lists show the categories in which a court writer represented religious wealth. They are not independently audited inventories, and the passage’s apparently impossible details should not be silently converted into architectural fact.[1]

No surviving modern photograph of Mathura’s ghats can show this central temple as it stood in 1018. Later paintings and present-day riverfront views can illustrate the city’s enduring setting, provided their captions state their dates. They should not be used to make an unsupported identification of the attacked building.

The order to burn and level the temples

Al-Utbi states that Mahmud ordered the temples burned with naphtha and fire and levelled to the ground. This is a direct report of deliberate destruction of religious buildings, made by a writer who approved of the campaign. It should not be softened into an unspecified “visit” or reduced to the taking of movable wealth alone.[1]

At the same time, the statement is a textual claim whose exact extent cannot be measured simply by repeating the word “all.” The inspected passage does not provide a plan matching each destroyed building to an excavated site. We can report the order and the chronicler’s representation of its execution without claiming a complete archaeological reconstruction of the city afterward.

The attack joined appropriation and destruction. Precious objects were described as convertible into weighed metal, while the buildings that gave them a sacred setting were burned. For worshippers, the loss was therefore not just financial: it damaged the places and objects through which religious life was organised.

Religious hostility is explicit in the court narrative, but it operated with practical incentives. The seizure of bullion, gems, elephants, and captives rewarded the army and reinforced royal power. An interpretation that excludes either declared iconoclasm or material extraction would leave out evidence the source itself supplies.

Kannauj: fortifications, flight, and plunder

After Mathura, the army proceeded toward Kannauj. The narrative gives 8 Shaban 409 AH for arrival, reconstructed as 20 December 1018. Al-Utbi says the ruler had fled across the Ganges, leaving the invaders to approach a complex of seven forts associated with the river.[1][2]

The ruler’s name is a problem in the old translation. Al-Utbi appears as naming a Rai Jaipal, while the historical ruler of Kannauj in this context is usually identified as Rajyapala. The translated form must not be used to merge him with the Shahi rulers of the northwest. The source’s naming difficulty and the identification made by modern historians are separate matters.[1][2]

Al-Utbi says the seven forts were taken in one day and that Mahmud allowed his soldiers to plunder and take prisoners. He describes inhabitants fleeing, being scattered, or killed if they did not escape. Again, this is the victorious chronicler’s account; it does not supply a complete population register or distinguish every civilian from every combatant.[1]

The text also claims nearly ten thousand temples at Kannauj. That number should not become a verified count of separate monumental buildings. It expresses the chronicler’s picture of a great religious centre and may include categories not recoverable from the English wording. Its rhetorical scale does not need to be accepted literally to recognise the significance of the reported assault on the city.

Flight by the ruler did not protect the inhabitants from plunder. The passage therefore resists an easy division between places that fought and places that submitted or were abandoned. Royal survival, military resistance, and the treatment of residents were related but different questions.

Munj and Asi: violence beyond the two famous cities

The expedition continued through other fortified places. Al-Utbi calls Munj a Brahman stronghold and describes opposition followed by desperate flight from high openings and battlements, with many deaths. The brief account should not be expanded into a detailed reconstruction of ritual suicide or a precise catalogue of victims that the source does not provide.[1]

At Asi, the chronicler describes a ruler called Chandal Bhor, a forested defensive setting, and extensive ditches. The ruler fled. Mahmud then ordered the destruction of five forts, and the narrative explicitly connects demolition with inhabitants buried in the ruins, while members of the garrison were killed, plundered, or imprisoned.[1]

These are severe claims, not merely an announcement that territory changed hands. They also remain claims transmitted in a celebratory account. There is no inspected excavation report here demonstrating the fate of each fort or allowing a casualty total to be assigned to the ruins.

The lesser-known places matter because the campaign’s effects extended beyond Mathura and Kannauj. A title centred on famous cities can conceal the sequence of attacks, pursuits, and local collapses along the way. The army’s return wealth accumulated through several episodes rather than a single isolated seizure.

Sharwa and the politics of flight

Al-Utbi’s account of Chand Rai at Sharwa introduces relationships among regional rulers. It describes earlier warfare, an attempted marriage alliance involving a son called Bhimpal, and detention after the proposed alliance. Names and identifications are difficult, but the narrative clearly portrays a region of rival courts rather than one coordinated defensive command.[1]

Advice to flee from Mahmud appears in a letter attributed to Bhimpal. Like other letters embedded in medieval chronicles, it should be read as a text transmitted by the author, not assumed to be an independently surviving original document. It shows how the chronicler represented Mahmud’s reputation as a force shaping local decisions.

Chand Rai withdrew with treasure and elephants into difficult country. Mahmud captured the fort but remained dissatisfied because the ruler had escaped. He pursued through forest and stony ground. The account dates the attack on the fleeing party to shortly before midnight on 25 Shaban, rendered as 6 January 1019.[1]

Al-Utbi describes killing and captivity in the surprise attack, followed by days spent searching bodies for valuables. This is not a harmless recovery of abandoned property. The source explicitly joins the pursuit of a ruler and his wealth to lethal violence against the group caught with him.

Its story of elephants approaching Mahmud almost voluntarily turns captured animals into signs of divine favour. That literary flourish should remain recognisable as the chronicler’s interpretation. It cannot establish that the animals understood or chose a religious allegiance.

Captives became merchandise

The concluding account of prisoners is among the most important passages in the campaign narrative. Al-Utbi says captives were sold for between two and ten dirhams, taken to Ghazna, and purchased by merchants arriving from distant cities. He describes their dispersal into Transoxiana, Iraq, and Khurasan.[1]

These are reported prices, not a complete market series. They cannot be converted responsibly into a precise present-day currency value without assumptions the passage does not support. Their significance is the chronicler’s claim that people had become so plentiful as saleable captives that the price was low.

The source explicitly presents rich and poor, and people of different appearance, as reduced to a common condition of slavery. That is a social consequence beyond the temporary capture of soldiers on a battlefield. Personal status, family connection, and local standing could be broken when people were removed and sold.[1]

The text does not name those individuals or tell us each eventual destination. It does not permit a confident account of every occupation, household, or later generation. But these limits should not become an excuse to hide slavery behind “booty.” The involuntary transfer and sale of people are precisely what the account describes.

The markets also show the campaign’s geographic reach. Violence in the Ganges–Yamuna region could supply people to purchasers across a much wider political and commercial world. An army’s return to Ghazna was therefore not the end of the captives’ displacement; it could be a stage in further forced movement.

What the campaign achieved—and what it did not establish

The expedition brought wealth, animals, prisoners, and prestige to Mahmud. It also left destroyed religious buildings, disrupted courts, deaths, flight, and enslavement in the places attacked. Al-Utbi’s celebratory account provides evidence of both sides of that outcome, even though it values them very differently from the communities that suffered.[1]

It does not prove continuous Ghaznavid administration over every city reached. A raid could penetrate far, devastate a place, and withdraw without creating a stable province. The later politics of Kannauj and the Chandelas make that distinction especially important. Military devastation did not end every regional contest or establish a single durable settlement for the entire plain.[2]

The campaign also demonstrates why original sources should be read explicitly. Their evidence supports the burning of temples, killings, captivity, and slave sales. Their enormous totals, confused names, religious insults, and literary miracles require scrutiny. Accuracy depends on preserving both the disturbing actions and the limits of what can be established about them.

Continue with the post-Kannauj and Chandela campaign dossier, or return to the guide to Mahmud’s invasions to compare this expedition with those in the northwest and Gujarat.

II (1869), printed pp. 41–50: river crossings and Baran, pp. 41–43; Kulchand, p. 43; Mathura, pp. 44–45; Kannauj, pp. 45–46; Munj and Asi, pp. 46–47; Chand Rai and Sharwa, pp. 47–49; prices, sale, and dispersal of captives, p. 50. Near-contemporary court narrative, not an independently audited casualty or treasury record. Read the original-source translation.
  2. Muhammad Nazim, The Life and Times of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazna (1931), printed pp. 106–110 and notes: chronology, the itinerary, source comparison, and political identifications. The reconstruction uses al-Utbi, Gardizi, and later sources; works known only through its citations are not presented here as independently inspected. Read the scholarly reconstruction.

The Persian-mediated version is useful for comparison with the Arabic-derived extract and should not be silently treated as the identical textual tradition. Read the parallel full narrative.

title: After Kannauj: Mahmud, the Chandelas, and a disputed campaign, 1019–1021
excerpt: A river crossing, the death of a king, and a Chandela army appear in different accounts of Mahmud’s next advance. Reading the original narratives separately reveals both the violence and the uncertainty.
html:
The destruction of temples at Mathura and the plundering of Kannauj did not finish Mahmud of Ghazni’s wars in northern India. The next sequence of events involved surviving Shahi rulers, the politics of the middle Ganges plain, and a powerful Chandela kingdom farther south. Yet this is also where an apparently simple list of invasions becomes difficult to defend. One near-contemporary narrative describes a dangerous river crossing. Gardizi, consulted through Nazim, and much later histories preserve another strand concerning Chandela power. The later version describes an expedition against a ruler called Nanda after the king of Kannauj was killed for submitting to Mahmud. These accounts overlap, but they are not identical.[1][2][3]

This article belongs to the guide to Mahmud’s invasions. It follows the Mathura and Kannauj campaign of 1018–1019. The dates in the title deliberately express a range: a campaign placed in 410 AH by one later historian is placed in 412 AH by another, while al-Utbi’s surviving narrative supplies no year for its river action. The safe task is to explain what each account actually says before deciding how much of a single campaign can be reconstructed.[1]

The landscape after the raids

Mahmud had returned from his eastern expedition with wealth, elephants, and captives. Al-Utbi, a writer closely associated with the Ghaznavid court, describes the sale of prisoners and their dispersal into Khurasan, Iraq, and Transoxiana. He also presents the destruction of sacred buildings as a triumph of Islam. The consequences of the expedition were therefore not confined to the removal of treasure. People lost freedom, religious institutions lost buildings and possessions, and rulers had to make decisions under the demonstrated threat of another invasion.[2]

There was no single Indian government to negotiate for all these territories. The Shahi dynasty had fought the Ghaznavids in the northwest. Kannauj belonged to a different political setting. The Chandelas ruled from strongholds in the region now associated with Bundelkhand. A ruler’s submission, flight, or resistance could affect neighbours without giving those neighbours the same interests. A king who avoided immediate destruction by accepting Mahmud’s demands might appear dangerously accommodating to another power. Conversely, the claim that an enemy had killed a submissive ruler offered Mahmud a useful explanation for renewed intervention.[1]

The later story of punishment for Kannauj’s submission must be read against this fragmentation. It does not establish a united national command or a campaign fought on behalf of every religious community. It describes, through the language of its chroniclers, several competing courts and an invading ruler exploiting their relationships. The distinction matters because a retrospective map can make these powers look much more coordinated than the evidence allows.

A near-contemporary account: the river called Rahib

Al-Utbi’s account, translated in the nineteenth century by Elliot and Dowson, begins after another expedition against the Afghans. Mahmud turns toward Hind, granting protection to those who submit and killing those who oppose him. The historian says he obtains booty before reaching a river called the Rahib. Its depth and muddy bottom make crossing difficult; men remove their armour before entering the water.[2]

On the opposite bank stands a ruler named Puru Jaipal, with soldiers and elephants. This spelling belongs to the translated source. It should not be silently converted into whichever familiar ruler a modern narrative requires. Names and titles were transmitted through Arabic and Persian manuscripts, and the different versions of these campaigns repeatedly confuse or alter them. The nineteenth-century editors themselves struggled to reconcile the Jaipals who appear in the Shahi and Kannauj stories.[1]

The river separates two armies and gives the defending force a practical advantage. Mahmud’s soldiers cannot simply use their usual mounted charge while struggling through deep water. Al-Utbi says that inflated skins were prepared and that a first group of eight men crossed. The opposing ruler sent troops and five elephants to prevent their landing, but the swimmers’ archery defeated that attempt. More Ghaznavid soldiers then crossed, followed by the army.[2]

These details are valuable evidence of how the chronicler imagined and celebrated a difficult military operation. They identify an obstacle, a crossing method, an advance party, and support from the remaining force. But the numerical neatness of eight heroes and the claim that the whole army arrived without even a horse’s hair being harmed also belong to a victory narrative. The account is not a surviving operations report that can be checked against a defending commander’s version.

Once across, Mahmud orders a mounted attack. Al-Utbi says some opponents are killed, others captured, others wounded and asking for protection, and the rest dispersed. He reports the seizure of 270 elephants. That number should remain attached to the chronicler: it shows the place of elephants in the representation of success, but it is not an independently audited tally.[2]

What al-Utbi does not say

The absences are important. This account does not name a Chandela ruler called Nanda. It does not explain the campaign as revenge for the killing of Kannauj’s king. It does not say Mahmud stormed Kalinjar. It does not place this action securely in either 1019 or 1021. Gardizi and later material may illuminate these omissions, but it cannot be inserted into al-Utbi’s text and then cited as though he supplied the combined story.[1][2]

Even the river is uncertain. In their appendix, Elliot and Dowson discuss whether the Rahib should be identified with the Ramganga or the Sai. Other histories set a similar crossing on the Yamuna. A mistaken river identification changes the inferred route substantially. It can move an army from one side of the Ganges plain to another and alter which political centre seems to be threatened.[1]

Readers can therefore accept that the source reports a contested river crossing without pretending that every modern place on an illustrated route has been proved. A route line drawn with precision can conceal uncertainty rather than resolve it. Where the text is uncertain, a map should display a broad zone or alternative possibilities.

The later Chandela account

An earlier strand also survives. Gardizi, as discussed by Nazim from Zayn al-akhbar, pp. 76–78, names Ganda, records the demand for submission and conversion, and describes his night withdrawal and the taking of elephants. Thus the confrontation is not known only from late-sixteenth-century writing. Its reported numbers also vary: Gardizi’s version, through Nazim, gives 145,000 infantry where Nizam al-Din gives 105,000. Neither total is an independently verified muster. The following paragraphs examine the directly accessible later version separately; its overlap with the early strand does not remove the problem of aligning either account with al-Utbi’s undated Rahib action.[3]

Nizam al-Din Ahmad’s Tabaqat-i Akbari, written in the late sixteenth century, provides a different framework. In its account, Mahmud hears that a ruler called Nanda has killed the king of Kannauj because that king acknowledged and submitted to him. Mahmud consequently advances against Nanda’s territory. This author places the expedition in 410 AH.[1]

The story then includes another encounter with Puru Jaipal at the Yamuna. Eight Ghaznavid guards cross the river, throw the opposing army into confusion, and proceed against a town called Bari. Finding it undefended, they plunder it and pull down temples. The eight-man episode is conspicuously similar to the crossing in al-Utbi, but similarities do not settle whether the later writer has preserved additional information, relocated an older episode, or combined more than one event.[1]

Afterward Mahmud approaches Nanda. The later history gives Nanda an immense army: 36,000 horsemen, 105,000 infantry, and 640 elephants. It says Mahmud first sends an envoy demanding submission and acceptance of Islam. Nanda refuses. Mahmud views the army from an eminence, becomes troubled by its size, and prays for success.[1]

These troop figures and the description of Mahmud’s feelings should be attributed explicitly. They are not numbers from a contemporary muster roll or observations recorded by someone standing beside him. The scene serves a literary purpose: a threatening host makes the eventual outcome demonstrate divine favour. That does not require readers to dismiss every event, but it does require them to separate a possible campaign from the dramatic explanation attached to it centuries later.

Withdrawal rather than a documented decisive battle

The Tabaqat-i Akbari says Nanda leaves during the night with a small group, abandoning baggage and equipment. Mahmud, suspicious of an ambush, examines the ground before ordering plunder. The text reports that 580 elephants are taken in neighbouring woods and that the invaders return to Ghazna with booty.[1]

This is not a detailed account of a great pitched battle in which Mahmud annihilates the Chandela army. The central action is the opposing ruler’s withdrawal and the seizure of what remains. A story in which both rulers hesitate or avoid a full engagement should not be rewritten into an uncomplicated battlefield conquest. Equally, the withdrawal in the later account does not prove that no fighting occurred anywhere on the march: the same text describes violence at the river and the destruction of temples at Bari.

The reported elephants also require care. The source claims 640 in the army and 580 captured; the near-contemporary river narrative claims 270. Combining those totals would manufacture a larger haul that no single source reports. Choosing the most impressive number while suppressing the other account would be equally misleading. The differences are part of the evidence readers should see.

Nanda, Ganda, and Vidyadhara

Modern discussions connect this campaign with the Chandela rulers Ganda and Vidyadhara. The translated chronicles’ name Nanda cannot, by itself, determine which ruler held effective command or how authority passed between generations. Nor can a spelling resemblance substitute for inscriptions and dynastic chronology. The terms “Chandela campaign” and “Nanda in the later account” are consequently more secure here than an unqualified assertion that every source names the same individual.[1]

The king of Kannauj is another difficulty. The historical episode is often discussed in relation to Rajyapala, but al-Utbi’s rendered names in the preceding expedition are confusing. Elliot and Dowson even proposed a connection between the Shahi Jaipal tradition and Kannauj that should not be adopted merely because it appears in an old reference work. A nineteenth-century editor’s solution is a hypothesis, not an additional medieval witness.[1]

The story that the Kannauj ruler was punished for submitting also invites an attractive but hazardous simplification: that Mahmud immediately marched to avenge a loyal vassal. The later chronicle supplies that explanation. It does not provide a surviving letter of appeal, a contemporary treaty defining the relationship, or testimony from the Chandela court about its reason for war. The political motive can be reported as the tradition’s account, while its documentary limits remain visible.

Why the date remains disputed

Elliot and Dowson place this material under a thirteenth expedition dated 412 AH, while acknowledging that al-Utbi gives no year and Nizam al-Din gives 410 AH. They prefer the later dating associated with Firishta. They also discuss whether the river episode and a campaign toward Kalinjar were actually one expedition.[1]

Muhammad Nazim subsequently revisited this chronology using the near-contemporary Gardizi. His reconstruction places Mahmud’s departure in autumn 410 AH, or October 1019, and follows the expedition through the river encounter and confrontation with the Chandela force. This provides a stronger chronological basis than simply accepting the much later Firishta’s date. It makes 1019–1020 the preferable working date, while the title’s wider range alerts readers to the older disagreement and the unresolved alignment of all the narratives.[3]

Islamic lunar years do not correspond neatly to a single Common Era year. Differences of one AH year, alternative identifications of an episode, and winter campaigns spanning parts of two solar years can produce apparently contradictory modern lists. A chronology that prints “1019” beside a polished battle narrative may therefore look more settled than the underlying evidence.

The separate Gwalior and Kalinjar article covers the later expedition dated 1022–1023 in Nazim’s reconstruction. Keeping the episodes separate for reading does not mean the surviving evidence proves every boundary used in a traditional seventeen-invasion list.

Violence, submission, and the purposes of war

Both versions connect military movement with extraction. Al-Utbi describes booty, prisoners, and elephants; the later Chandela account describes plundered equipment and animals after a withdrawal. Both also frame the conflict religiously. The later account’s demand for conversion, and its description of temple destruction at Bari, cannot be removed without altering what the text says.[1][2]

These purposes were capable of operating together. Taking elephants could strengthen subsequent campaigns. Seizing wealth rewarded an army and magnified royal power. Demanding submission weakened an opponent. Presenting destruction as a victory of faith legitimised the conqueror and gave his followers a language in which violence became merit. Readers do not have to choose a single motive that excludes all the others.

The human result is also clearer when administrative terms are made concrete. “Booty” could include a person. A prisoner might be sold away from home; an elephant represented the forced transfer of a major resource; a burned temple meant lost possessions and damaged worship as well as a celebrated royal exploit. Al-Utbi’s approving tone does not erase these consequences. It makes the historian’s own position especially important to disclose.

At the same time, the evidence here is insufficient for a precise casualty total. The account of the river lists categories of killed, captured, and fleeing people without a reliable overall count. The later Chandela narrative’s huge army should not be transformed into an equally huge death toll. Explicit history names violence where it is reported and stops where the surviving evidence stops.

An unresolved episode in a continuing war

The most defensible reconstruction is limited but substantial: Ghaznavid pressure continued after Kannauj; a near-contemporary source describes a successful and violent river operation against a ruler rendered as Puru Jaipal; Gardizi, consulted through Nazim, and later histories connect renewed campaigning with Chandela power and the fate of Kannauj’s king. They disagree over dates and add details that cannot all be independently confirmed.[1][2]

The uncertainty does not make the campaign unimportant. It reveals how a court chronicle, later compilations, and modern numbered lists produce different kinds of historical knowledge. A reader who knows where a story comes from can recognise the difference between evidence of a reported action and evidence of how later generations wanted that action remembered.

Continue with the second Kashmir attempt and Lahore campaign, traditionally 1021, or return to the campaign guide to compare the sequence and its disputed boundaries.

Accessible full text with printed-page markers.
  2. Al-Utbi, Tarikh-i Yamini, extracts translated in Elliot and Dowson, vol. II, printed pp. 42–51, particularly pp. 50–51 for the river action and p. 50 for the preceding campaign’s slave sales. Near-contemporary court narrative; army and booty figures are its claims. Original-source extracts in translation.
  3. Muhammad Nazim, The Life and Times of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazna (1931), printed pp. 110–113 and notes, analysing Gardizi pp. 76–78 alongside al-Utbi and later accounts. Prefers autumn 1019/410 AH for the renewed campaign and distinguishes the earlier encounter from the later Kalinjar expedition. Scholarly chronological reconstruction.

title: The fortress Mahmud could not take: Kashmir and Lahore, 1021–1022
excerpt: Mahmud’s second attempt to enter Kashmir ended before Lohkot. A failed siege, the winter landscape, and the return toward Lahore expose the limits of conquest behind the court’s victories.
html:
Mahmud of Ghazni’s campaigns were devastating, but they were not an uninterrupted succession of conquered kingdoms. Kashmir presents a particularly clear limit. In the campaign conventionally dated 1021–1022, he again approached the mountain fortress called Lohkot. He failed to take it, abandoned the siege, and returned toward the Punjab. The valley beyond did not become his conquest.[1][2]

This was his second attempt, following the first Kashmir campaign of 1015–1016. It comes after the disputed Chandela and river campaign in the guide to Mahmud’s invasions. Its importance lies partly in what the result forces us to acknowledge: a powerful army could inflict immense damage in the plains and still fail against a defended approach into the mountains.

Two attempts, not one victory

The chronology is easily blurred. A first attempt is placed in 406 AH, corresponding to the campaign of late 1015 and early 1016. A second belongs to 412 AH, beginning in the autumn of 1021 and ending with a return to Ghazna in spring 1022. Muhammad Nazim’s scholarly reconstruction distinguishes them using Gardizi, the near-contemporary author of the Zayn al-akhbar.[2]

Gardizi is especially important because al-Utbi does not supply a full narrative of either unsuccessful expedition. That silence should not become an excuse to omit the failures. Court history has uneven coverage: a source exceptionally useful for descriptions of victory can be much less informative about an unsuccessful siege. Other evidence must carry the story, with the route by which it reaches us made clear.

The distinction also prevents an opposite mistake: placing the same defeat twice merely because later authors repeat a familiar motif. In this case Nazim specifically reads Gardizi as recording two attempts separated by several years. The second revisited a barrier that had already stopped Mahmud. That is a more precise proposition than saying he repeatedly invaded “Kashmir” without explaining whether he entered its central valley.[2]

What Lohkot guarded

In the reconstructed route, Lohkot was a fortified obstacle on an approach into Kashmir, associated with the modern Loharin area and the Toshamaidan route. The identification draws on historical geography, not on the assumption that any present-day fort sharing a similar name must be the same place. Nazim cites Gardizi and Kalhana’s form Loharakotta; he also relies on Aurel Stein’s study of Kashmir’s routes.[2]

The military problem was greater than a wall. An attacking force needed a usable approach, food for soldiers, forage for animals, room to deploy, and a way to preserve communication with its base. A position commanding a mountain entrance could interrupt those requirements without ever meeting the invader on an open plain. The fact that an army could approach a fortress did not mean it could move its full force past it.

Al-Biruni’s near-contemporary description helps recover that geographical setting. In India, he describes Kashmir as a plateau enclosed by high and difficult mountains. He emphasises the inhabitants’ care over entrances and roads. He also discusses the limited access given to outsiders and the difficulty of commerce. These passages are not a narrative of Mahmud’s siege, but they independently show why the approaches mattered so much.[3]

His travel geography should not be mistaken for a modern military map. Some names and distances require interpretation, and his general statements cannot establish the position of every camp. Their value is more fundamental: Kashmir’s protection depended on controlling a small number of difficult passages, a condition an invader could not remove simply by having won previous battles elsewhere.

The first failure remained relevant

The earlier siege had already revealed the problem. As reconstructed from Gardizi, Mahmud invested Lohkot, but heavy snow interfered with communication. After about a month the attempt was abandoned. Accounts of the difficult withdrawal include loss of direction and danger from water; the relationship among the later versions is not completely simple. The basic result, however, is clear: the fortress was not reduced and the invasion failed.[2]

That earlier experience gives the second attempt its significance. Mahmud was not encountering an entirely unknown barrier in 1021. He was returning to an obstacle that had resisted him. It is reasonable to infer that the route remained strategically important, but there is no need to invent a private vow of revenge, a council speech, or a detailed siege plan that the surviving texts do not preserve.

The intervening years had also shown the reach of his power in other directions. The Mathura and Kannauj expedition carried his army deep into the northern plains. That success did not automatically solve the mountain problem. Operational experience in one landscape did not remove the defensive advantage of another.

Autumn 1021: the second approach

Nazim dates the renewed expedition to September–October 1021, in 412 AH, citing Gardizi. The second siege again lasts approximately a month in that account. The fortress’s natural defences cannot be overcome. Severe winter conditions then worsen the attackers’ position, and Mahmud raises the siege.[2]

The seasonal setting is meaningful, but it does not license picturesque invention. We do not possess a day-by-day diary describing every snowfall or a reliable list of men who died outside the walls. A historical account can state that winter and the defended site obstructed the expedition without adding imagined frozen bodies, speeches by starving soldiers, or precise casualty totals.

The army’s withdrawal should also be described as a failed siege, not softened into a successful reconnaissance. Whatever other operations followed in the Punjab, the immediate objective at Lohkot was not achieved. Conversely, the failure does not prove that Mahmud’s army was annihilated or that its entire military system collapsed. He returned and campaigned again. The evidence supports a significant local defeat of purpose within an empire that remained powerful.

Lahore and the winter in the Punjab

Following the failed attempt, the army returned toward Lahore and the sub-Himalayan Punjab. Nazim notes Gardizi’s reference to Lahore and a region rendered Takeshar, associating the latter with the hill country of the western Punjab. His reconstruction puts Mahmud’s return to Ghazna at the beginning of spring, March–April 1022.[2]

The distinction between retreating to a wintering region and capturing a city is essential. A phrase saying that the ruler returned to Lahore does not by itself prove that Lahore was first conquered during that exact movement. The Shahi position in the Punjab had been eroded through earlier fighting, displacement, tribute, and Ghaznavid intervention. A single dramatic “fall of Lahore” can conceal a more extended process.

The much later Tabaqat-i Akbari, quoted by Elliot and Dowson, describes a month before Lohkot, withdrawal toward Lahore and Bagar, and orders to plunder the hill country. It says immense booty was collected. This passage supplies an explicit tradition of predation after the failed siege. It does not convert the failure into the conquest of Kashmir.[1]

Plunder should not be treated as a neutral consolation prize. It meant that the ability to resist a fortress assault did not protect every neighbouring settlement or household from an army returning through the region. At the same time, the quoted passage does not give a reliable list of affected villages, a captive total, or a casualty count. Those details cannot be supplied merely to make the account more dramatic.

A composite campaign in the later histories

Some older lists place Kirat, Nur, Lohkot, and Lahore together as a single expedition. Elliot and Dowson’s appendix does so, under a heading dated 413 AH, while discussing place names and extracting a narrative from Nizam al-Din Ahmad. The sequence includes the submission of one mountain chief, an expedition against another district, construction of a fort, conversion, and then the Kashmir attempt.[1]

That arrangement needs qualification. Nazim treats the Nur and Kirat operations separately and argues that the second Kashmir expedition belongs to 412 AH, not the appendix’s 413. He specifically warns that linking the Kashmir siege as a sequel to those valley operations lacks authority in the evidence he uses.[2]

The resulting uncertainty affects more than a date. If several operations were compressed into one heading by a later compiler, an article that gives Mahmud a seamless march through all four places may create a route that no near-contemporary source records. Keeping the reader’s article focused on the second Kashmir attempt and Punjab return preserves what can be supported while acknowledging the older composite list.

This is also why traditional numbered campaigns should function as a reading guide rather than a claim that medieval officials maintained the same seventeen-item catalogue. Sources group events differently; modern authors make additional decisions about what constitutes an invasion. The numbering can be useful without making those editorial choices invisible.

Religion and coercion in the surrounding accounts

The later narrative of Nur and Kirat explicitly describes idol worship, acceptance of Islam, appointment of a Muslim governor, and the spread of Islam by both consent and force. These are claims in a late-sixteenth-century history. They should be presented as such, rather than imported into the Lohkot siege as if they were a contemporary report of conversions inside Kashmir.[1]

Nor does the failure to enter the valley imply that the wider conflict lacked a religious language. Mahmud’s court historians repeatedly praised his campaigns as struggles against unbelief, and the destruction or removal of sacred images was part of his public reputation. The task is to identify where a specific account actually documents those acts. For this siege there is no basis for claiming that he destroyed all Kashmir’s temples or imposed a new religious order throughout the valley.

The distinction protects the history from both evasion and exaggeration. Violence elsewhere in the campaign sequence is amply documented. Here, the central fact is the survival of a defended entrance against him. One outcome should not be overwritten to make the whole career fit an unbroken story of either triumph or failure.

What the defenders achieved

For the defenders, holding Lohkot denied Mahmud the route he sought. Fortification and terrain forced him into a time-consuming operation and exposed the besiegers to a worsening season. The surviving narrative gives less attention to the defenders’ organisation than to Mahmud’s movement, but their success is visible in the result.[1][2]

It would be tempting to fill that imbalance with a heroic commander’s invented speech or a precise tactical plan. The better response is to acknowledge the missing perspective. We know a defended position remained untaken; we do not know every order issued within it. Recognising that gap does not diminish the achievement. It prevents the modern account from replacing a source’s silence with fiction.

Kashmir’s political independence also cannot be reduced to geography alone. Mountain entrances were useful because people maintained and defended them. Al-Biruni’s remarks on guarded roads underline that relationship between terrain and organised control. A mountain range is not automatically a functioning defensive system; the sources describe a society attentive to the points where outsiders could enter.[3]

The limits of a conqueror’s reach

The campaign ended with Mahmud outside Kashmir’s central valley and returning through a Punjab increasingly exposed to Ghaznavid power. It demonstrates a mixed outcome: failure at the fortified entrance, continued capacity for movement and plunder elsewhere, and no permanent conquest of the valley.[1][2]

The distinction is visible even within the comparatively short later account. Its sequence moves from an untaken fortress to plunder collected elsewhere and finally a return home. Those stages could all be narrated as part of one royal expedition, yet they describe different military results. The valley’s successful defence did not guarantee security for the Punjab; the army’s plunder in the Punjab did not undo the valley’s successful defence. Reading the sequence in that form restores the uneven geography of power that a single coloured area on a map can obscure.[1]

Such a result matters to the interpretation of his reign. Royal titles and chronicles could describe sweeping dominion, but effective control varied sharply from place to place. Raiding, tributary arrangements, garrisons, and the ability to pass an army through a district were different relationships. None should be treated as interchangeable with ruling every region that appeared in a victory narrative.

Continue with Gwalior and Kalinjar, 1022–1023, where the surviving accounts describe negotiations and elephants rather than a demonstrable storming of the great fortresses. The campaign guide places both episodes in the wider sequence and marks the uncertainties in their traditional numbering.

Sources

  1. Nizam al-Din Ahmad, Tabaqat-i Akbari, late-sixteenth-century narrative quoted in H. M. Elliot and John Dowson, The History of India as Told by Its Own Historians, vol. II (1869), Appendix Note D, printed pp. 464–467. The appendix combines Kirat, Nur, Lohkot and Lahore and discusses place-name problems; its dates and combinations need checking against earlier evidence. Translated passages and editorial comparison.
  2. Muhammad Nazim, The Life and Times of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazna (1931), printed pp. 74–75 and 104–105 and notes, using Gardizi pp. 72–73 and 79 to distinguish the two sieges and date the second to 412 AH/1021–1022. This is modern scholarship transmitting and analysing the earlier evidence; Gardizi’s original has not been presented here as a directly inspected English text. Scholarly reconstruction and source references.
  3. Al-Biruni, India, trans. Eduard C. Sachau (1888; reissued 1910), vol. I, chapter XVIII, printed pp. 206–208: Kashmir’s mountains, guarded entrances, limited access, and regional travel geography. A near-contemporary geographical description, not an eyewitness siege report. Digitised original-source translation.

title: Gwalior and Kalinjar, 1022–1023: elephants, sieges, and negotiated power
excerpt: Mahmud’s return to Chandela territory brought pressure on two great hill forts. The sources describe elephants and a negotiated settlement, while later storytelling can make an agreement look like a conquest.
html:
The expedition against Gwalior and Kalinjar presents a different outcome from the burning of Mathura or the attack on Somnath. Here, the surviving accounts describe strong fortresses, siege pressure, elephants offered as the price of peace, and the withdrawal of the invading army. Mahmud of Ghazni could claim submission and valuable resources, but the evidence does not justify saying that he stormed and permanently occupied both great forts.[1][2]

This article continues the guide to Mahmud’s invasions, following the second Kashmir attempt and Punjab return of 1021–1022. The campaign is commonly dated to 1022–1023. Its relationship with the earlier Chandela confrontation of 1019–1020 is important: the first encounter had not eliminated the power of the rulers south of the Ganges plain.[2]

Why return to Chandela territory?

The earlier expedition left a powerful opponent in place. In the later Persian narrative this ruler is called Nanda; modern historical reconstruction connects the episode with the Chandela dynasty and the names Ganda and Vidyadhara. The transmission of names is difficult, and the translated chronicles do not warrant treating every spelling as a precise identification of the same individual.[1][2]

What matters for the campaign is that the political centre had survived. A raid could obtain booty and elephants without removing the ruler or occupying his principal fortresses. An army returning to Ghazna with trophies did not necessarily leave an obedient government behind. Continued resistance or refusal to meet demands could therefore draw another expedition.

Nazim’s reconstruction explicitly says that the earlier campaign had not broken the Chandela ruler’s power. Using Gardizi, he places the renewed advance in 413 AH, corresponding to 1022, and the return in spring 1023. This reading is more coherent than the inconsistent dates printed in the nineteenth-century compilation, whose heading gives 414 AH while its quoted passage gives 413.[1][2]

A date difference should not distract from the more consequential question: what kind of victory was achieved? A conquered fortress, an intimidated ruler, an annual tributary promise, and an immediate gift of elephants are related but distinct outcomes. The sources’ own descriptions make that distinction possible.

Gwalior: an obstacle on the approach

The account places Gwalior before Kalinjar. In Nazim’s reconstruction, its ruler is a subordinate of the Chandela power and holds a fortress on a steep rock. Mahmud attacks but cannot take it. After four days, the local ruler seeks peace and offers 35 elephants.[2]

The Tabaqat-i Akbari passage quoted by Elliot and Dowson similarly describes a siege and a settlement after four days, with 35 elephants promised in return for protection. The relatively brief text does not give a detailed account of breaches, ladders, mining, or an assault through a gate. Those familiar siege details should not be supplied simply because a modern article needs a dramatic battle scene.[1]

A ruler could resist successfully at the walls and still judge a negotiated payment preferable to a longer siege. Fortification protected a position, but it did not make the surrounding countryside, supply routes, and dependants invulnerable. The sources do not preserve the full calculations of Gwalior’s ruler. They do, however, describe an agreement instead of the fortress’s destruction.

The number of elephants remains a source report. It is less extravagant than some of the enormous totals in the campaign traditions, but modest appearance is not independent verification. It should be written as “the account reports 35 elephants,” rather than converted into a precise modern valuation or treated as a surviving treasury receipt.

What an elephant payment meant

Elephants appear so frequently in these narratives that they can become decorative symbols of medieval India. In these transactions they were material resources. An animal suitable for military use represented training, handlers, provisioning, and the ability to sustain a costly force. Transferring elephants could benefit the recipient’s army while reducing the donor’s resources.

Their appearance also served political storytelling. A chronicler could measure a ruler’s submission through visible animals delivered to the victorious camp. A herd made a royal success tangible in a way that a vague promise of friendship did not. This is why the reported numbers deserve attention even when their exact accuracy cannot be proved.

The distinction between payment and conquest remains essential. Receiving animals did not necessarily give Mahmud the power to appoint every officer, collect every local tax, or keep a permanent garrison inside the fort. If a history claims all of those consequences, it needs additional evidence. The elephant transaction alone cannot supply them.

Kalinjar: siege pressure without a documented storming

Mahmud next proceeds to Kalinjar. The fortress’s strength dominates the accounts. Nizam al-Din Ahmad calls it exceptional among the strongholds of Hindustan. Nazim, drawing on Gardizi and other material, describes a siege intended to close approaches and compel the defenders through shortage.[1][2]

A blockade was an attempt to make a defensive advantage costly over time. A wall might stop an assault while the garrison still depended on stored food, water arrangements, and continued political support. Yet the surviving narrative here does not establish how completely Mahmud closed the approaches or how near the defenders came to exhaustion. The historical statement should therefore remain that he laid siege and sought submission, not that starvation inside the fort has been documented household by household.

The settlement is the key event. The ruler offers 300 elephants and seeks peace. Mahmud accepts and raises the siege. In Nazim’s account the arrangement also includes a promise of annual tribute. Whatever degree of compulsion produced it, this was a negotiation between an invading army and a ruling power that remained capable of bargaining.[1][2]

Calling the outcome merely a friendly exchange would conceal the armed pressure. Calling it the complete destruction of Kalinjar would contradict the account’s form. The sources describe a threatened stronghold purchasing or negotiating relief, while Mahmud converts the siege into a claim of successful submission.

The riderless elephants

One memorable detail says that the elephants were sent out without riders. The Ghaznavid soldiers seized and mounted them. In the Tabaqat-i Akbari narrative, the defenders are surprised by this display. Gardizi, as transmitted through Nazim’s discussion, also provides the riderless-elephant story.[1][2]

The scene presents military nerve as a form of mastery. Elephants that might have been dangerous become another opportunity for the invader’s men to demonstrate superiority. It is also the kind of vivid episode that later authors could embroider. Nazim specifically objects to a claim that the elephants were intoxicated: the earlier authority he cites does not support it.[2]

The difference is small in wording and large in effect. Riderless elephants are the reported diplomatic delivery; deliberately maddened elephants would imply a concealed trap and an additional heroic ordeal. Adding the latter makes the story more exciting by changing the evidence. It should not appear in a factual reconstruction unless its later source and uncertain status are explained.

We also lack an independent record from the defenders explaining their purpose. Sending the animals without handlers may have had practical or ceremonial meanings that a victorious court’s account does not preserve. It is safest to state the reported action and the chronicler’s interpretation separately.

A Hindi poem in a Ghaznavid victory narrative

The account then turns from elephants to verse. Nanda sends a Hindi poem praising Mahmud. The sultan has it examined by learned men and poets associated with his court, receives their favourable judgment, and rewards the author. The translated chronicle reports a grant or confirmation involving 15 forts and further presents.[1]

This scene matters because it records diplomacy conducted through people able to interpret an Indian language within the Ghaznavid court’s world. The relation between the two sides was not maintained solely by a battle cry or a blow. Envoys, interpreters, poems, gifts, and the conferral of honours also gave shape to power.

The poem itself is not preserved in the cited passage. We cannot quote lines from it, name its original metre, or reconstruct the author’s feelings. Praise offered under military pressure does not prove personal admiration; it can be a diplomatic act. Nor does a reported reward settle what authority Mahmud actually possessed over each of the 15 forts.

The statement is best treated as part of the settlement tradition. It suggests a ruler acknowledging the invader sufficiently to end the immediate threat, while the victorious narrative depicts Mahmud as able to confer honours. Both sides could have had reasons to accept an arrangement that could be represented differently at their own courts.

The question of lasting control

The distinction between a claim of overlordship and sustained administration is central to this expedition. A promise of tribute could mark subordination, but the durability of such promises depended on enforcement, local politics, and the ruler’s ability to return. The survival of the Chandela centre after the campaign cautions against colouring an entire region as a permanently administered Ghaznavid province on the basis of this one settlement.[2]

The sources used here describe Mahmud’s return to Ghazna. They do not provide a detailed occupation regime for Kalinjar, a complete replacement of its governing elite, or the destruction of its entire defensive system. A map caption saying “area raided or subjected to demands” can therefore be more accurate than one saying “territory annexed.”

This does not make the expedition harmless. The demand was backed by an army capable of violence, and the transfer of valuable resources reduced the defender’s freedom of action. Submission negotiated under siege was a coercive political relationship. Its coercion should be visible without attributing to it every consequence of a permanent conquest.

What can be said about destruction and captivity?

In other campaigns, al-Utbi explicitly celebrates killing, temple burning, and the sale of captives. The passages central to Gwalior and Kalinjar emphasise siege and settlement instead. They do not supply a documented massacre inside either surrendered fortress or a reliable total of people enslaved there.[1]

That difference should be respected. It would be wrong to infer that Mahmud had abandoned the religious and fiscal purposes evident elsewhere. It would also be wrong to copy the atrocities of Mathura or Somnath into Kalinjar simply because the same invader was involved. Each episode requires its own evidence.

The narrative still contains the threat of destructive force, and negotiations happened in its presence. The fact that a siege ended in payment rather than a storm could itself have spared people from the forms of killing and capture that the court histories praise in other places. The record does not let us count those spared, and it should not be made to do so.

Reading the sources at different distances

The most easily accessible full passage is in the late-sixteenth-century Tabaqat-i Akbari, quoted by Elliot and Dowson. Its distance from the campaign is substantial. Nearer evidence matters, which is why Nazim’s references to Gardizi are useful. This article distinguishes directly inspected translated passages from early material encountered through a modern scholar’s analysis.[1][2]

Al-Utbi’s absence is also relevant. His surviving Indian narrative does not give this campaign the coverage found in the earlier Mathura expedition. A modern writer cannot fill the gap by transferring one of his descriptions of temple destruction to a later year. The uneven survival and selection of texts set real limits on detail.

The old compilation’s inconsistent AH heading offers a warning about dates as well. Quoting a printed source accurately does not mean repeating every editorial error it contains. A historical account should explain which chronology it adopts and why, while retaining the original wording where the disagreement matters.

A settlement before Somnath

The expedition traditionally ends with Mahmud returning in the spring of 1023. He had obtained elephant payments and a submission that could be celebrated at Ghazna. Gwalior and Kalinjar had faced armed coercion, but their fortresses were not shown by this evidence to have been annihilated or permanently occupied.[2]

The contrast with the next major expedition is striking because it is supported by the sources. At Kalinjar, the account centres on a ruler and an agreement. At Somnath in 1025–1026, near-contemporary evidence explicitly records destruction of the sacred image and its removal to Ghazna, while a later narrative describes the assault and heavy slaughter. These outcomes should be compared with their differences intact.

Return to the campaign guide to follow the wider chronology, or continue to Somnath for a campaign whose religious significance, violence, and later legends have often been collapsed into one story.

Sources

II (1869), Appendix Note D, printed pp. 467–468: Gwalior, Kalinjar, elephant payments, Hindi verse and the reported reward. The heading and quoted passage give different AH years. Original-source passage in translation.
  2. Muhammad Nazim, The Life and Times of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazna (1931), printed pp. 110–114, especially pp. 113–114 and notes, using Gardizi pp. 79–80 and other early material. Supports the 413 AH/1022–1023 reconstruction and distinguishes the riderless-elephant account from an unsupported intoxication detail. A modern analysis with explicit medieval source references.
