title: Somnath, 1025–1026: the assault, the shattered linga, and the sources
excerpt: Mahmud crossed the desert to attack Somnath and carried its broken sacred image to Ghazna. Near-contemporary testimony, later siege narratives, and the ordeal of the return reveal a history more disturbing and more complex than the familiar legends.
html:
In January 1026, Mahmud of Ghazni’s army reached Somnath on the coast of western India. The sacred image was broken, its valuable coverings taken, and portions carried to Ghazna. There they were placed in public settings designed to advertise the conqueror’s triumph: the hippodrome and the entrance of a mosque, where people wiped their feet. This destruction and deliberate humiliation of a sacred object are recorded by al-Biruni, a scholar writing close to the events.[1]

The fighting surrounding that destruction is described most fully in a later narrative. Ibn al-Athir, writing roughly two centuries afterward, tells of assaults on the walls, killing at the temple gate, and fugitives overtaken at sea. His reported death toll of more than 50,000 is famous. It is a medieval historian’s claim, however, not a contemporary count of the dead. Keeping these different kinds of evidence separate allows the violence to be stated plainly without turning every later embellishment into fact.[1][2]

Somnath forms the sixteenth dossier in the guide to Mahmud’s invasions, following the Gwalior and Kalinjar expedition of 1022–1023. It was followed by a punishing journey through western India and Sind, and later by the campaign against the Jats, conventionally dated 1027.

A shrine beside an ocean route

Somnath was a place of worship, but its setting also belonged to the maritime world of the Indian Ocean. Al-Biruni explains its fame partly through its harbour and its role as a station for people travelling between Sufala in the country of the Zanj and China. His description places the shrine within a network of movement and exchange extending far beyond a single kingdom.[1]

The name, in his explanation, means “lord of the moon.” He identifies the sacred object as the linga of Mahadeva and recounts the religious story connecting its worship with the moon. He also describes offerings brought from distant places: water from the Ganges and flowers from Kashmir. These details convey the shrine’s reach through devotion as well as geography.[1]

Ibn al-Athir’s later account presents the institution on a grand scale. He reports endowments from more than 10,000 villages, extensive treasure, a thousand Brahmans involved in worship, attendants serving pilgrims, and musicians and dancers. The exact figures cannot be independently verified from his account. They nevertheless show the kind of wealthy religious establishment that later historians believed Mahmud had attacked.[2]

There is a crucial difference between describing that institution and reducing it to a storehouse waiting to be seized. Its wealth was attached to worship, offerings, employment, journeys, and the prestige of a sacred place. To attack it was to damage those relationships as well as to obtain material resources. The removal of a linga to a mosque threshold made the religious meaning of the act particularly explicit.

Why Mahmud went so far

Mahmud already had a record of attacking sacred institutions and bringing wealth and images back to Ghazna. The bronze Cakrasvamin taken from Thanesar later lay alongside a portion of the Somnath image, according to al-Biruni. The two objects became parts of the same public language of victory, even though their original religious identities differed.[1]

Ibn al-Athir supplies a particular explanation for the new expedition. He says Hindus attributed Mahmud’s destruction of other images to Somnath’s displeasure with those deities. Mahmud therefore resolved to destroy Somnath too, expecting the failure of its protection to encourage conversion. This is the later historian’s account of the motive, not a surviving transcript of a decision made in the sultan’s presence.[2]

The religious purpose described by the chronicles can coexist with the pursuit of wealth and prestige. A rich shrine offered portable valuables; a distant expedition offered an exceptional feat to celebrate; destruction of a famous sacred object could demonstrate the king’s proclaimed defence of Islam. The sources give no reason to erase any of these purposes in favour of a single exclusive explanation.

The distance also made the undertaking risky. An army crossing dry country needed water and food not only for its soldiers but for a large train of animals. A campaign that succeeded at its destination could still be damaged on the way home. The history of Somnath includes both the conquest and that exposed return.

From Ghazna to Multan

The accepted chronology places Mahmud’s departure from Ghazna in the autumn of 1025 and the attack in January 1026. Al-Biruni independently dates the destruction to 416 AH. Muhammad Nazim’s reconstruction, using several medieval accounts, places the departure in October and the halt at Multan in November.[1][3]

The old English translation of Ibn al-Athir quoted by Elliot and Dowson prints 414 AH in the narrative, despite the appendix’s own heading placing the expedition in 416–417. That printed date should not be used to move the assault two years earlier. The near-contemporary chronological anchor is 416 AH; the later detailed story must be read with its transmission problems acknowledged.[1][2][3]

Multan was a base for preparing the desert crossing. The later account gives 30,000 mounted men in addition to volunteers and describes large numbers of camels carrying water and grain. These reported totals are not certain statistics, but their central practical point is credible: the invaders could not depend on finding adequate supplies along an unprepared desert route.[2]

Water points consequently had military importance. In Ibn al-Athir’s narrative, a fort with wells is taken after the crossing begins. He says the inhabitants are killed and their images broken, and that the army carries water away before continuing. The well and the sacred image appear in the same episode: a logistical need and religiously celebrated destruction formed parts of one advance.[2]

Through Gujarat toward the coast

The army moved toward Anahilwara, the Chaulukya capital associated with Bhima. The later account says Bhima abandoned the city and sought safety in a fortress. Nazim reconstructs the refuge as Kanthkot in Kutch, while acknowledging and rejecting other proposed identifications in his discussion. The forms of the name vary in the translated texts.[2][3]

Bhima’s flight left Mahmud free to continue, but it did not mean every population on the route surrendered peacefully. Ibn al-Athir describes intermediate forts where people were killed, fortifications destroyed, and images broken. He also reports a force of 20,000 local fighting men defeated and dispersed, followed by the taking and plundering of Dabalwara near Somnath.[2]

These actions should not be hidden beneath the phrase “he marched to Somnath.” The advance itself, in this account, involved the destruction of places and the killing of people before the principal shrine came into view. At the same time, the text’s uncertain place names and rounded numbers limit the precision with which those episodes can be mapped.

The march brought a force from inland Afghanistan to a coastal settlement sustained by a very different geography. The final objective stood beside the sea, not behind an endless protective desert. What had impeded the invaders also made their progress a feat for their chroniclers to celebrate: Mahmud had carried an army across a difficult route to strike a distant centre of worship.

The assault on Somnath

Al-Biruni supplies an important distinction between the age of the sacred place and the age of its fortification. He says the fortress containing the image and its treasures had been built about a hundred years before his time. That is his historical information, not a modern archaeological dating, but it shows that his account did not treat every feature of the site as equally ancient. An established place of worship could acquire a comparatively recent defensive enclosure.[1]

The relationship between shrine and fortress also shaped what followed. Walls could protect the institution and its accumulated possessions; once the fighting passed them, defenders and worshippers could be compressed toward the sacred centre. The later narrative’s movement from ramparts to temple gate is therefore more than a change of scenery. It shows a defensive perimeter giving way and violence concentrating at the place the enclosure was meant to protect.[2]

The coast complicated escape in turn. The sea offered boats and the possibility of getting beyond the attacker’s immediate reach, but it could also expose fugitives to pursuit and drowning. The account describes both the walls and the water as elements of the struggle. It does not give a complete plan of the fortress or the position of every vessel, so the precise relationship of the buildings to the shore remains beyond this reconstruction.

Ibn al-Athir describes a strong fortress built beside the water, its walls washed by the sea. He says Mahmud arrived on a Thursday in the middle of Dhu'l Qa'da. The following day the assailants advanced, brought ladders to the walls, and gained a position above them. Fighting continued, and night interrupted the action.[2]

The source also supplies taunts from the defenders, who supposedly expected their deity to destroy the invaders. Such dialogue belongs to a later literary account of the siege. It can illuminate the religious framing of the story, but it should not be treated as words securely recorded from the ramparts.

On the next morning, the narrative says, the assault resumed. The defenders were driven toward the temple. Ibn al-Athir describes successive groups entering the shrine, praying, and returning to fight until they were killed. The gate became the setting for intense slaughter. The account presents the defenders’ religious attachment as central to their resistance, just as it presents the attackers’ action through the language of Islam.[2]

The chronology reconstructed by Nazim places these principal days on 7 and 8 January 1026. His analysis also uses Gardizi and other medieval material, rather than relying only on Ibn al-Athir. The precise progress of the fighting remains less securely recoverable than the fact that the shrine was attacked and its image destroyed.[3]

The dead and those who tried to escape

The later account does not end the violence when the walls are taken. It describes people fleeing in boats, pursued by the victors, with some killed and others drowned. Flight by water, which might otherwise have offered an exit from a coastal fortress, becomes another scene of death.[2]

Ibn al-Athir concludes with a reported total exceeding 50,000 slain. That figure has often migrated into modern histories without its source label. It should remain “Ibn al-Athir reports more than 50,000,” accompanied by the fact that he wrote much later and gives no independently verifiable counting method. Al-Biruni’s near-contemporary account of the destruction does not supply this casualty total.[1][2]

The uncertainty of a number does not make the reported slaughter unimportant. It changes what can honestly be claimed about its scale. Nor does the narrative allow everyone killed to be classified neatly as a professional soldier. Its defenders include people gathered around a sacred place, and its fugitives are not described through the categories a modern military census would require.

The cited siege narrative provides no reliable overall count of captives. Captivity was a recurring feature of Mahmud’s campaigns, but figures from Mathura or another expedition cannot be transferred to Somnath. The explicit evidence here concerns killing, drowning, plunder, and destruction of the sacred image.

Breaking the linga

Al-Biruni’s evidence is especially important at this point. He calls the object a linga of Mahadeva. He says Mahmud ordered its upper portion broken and the remainder transported to Ghazna, along with coverings and ornaments of gold, jewels, and embroidered garments.[1]

This description differs from the familiar image of a human-shaped idol smashed open to reveal a hidden chamber of jewels. A solid stone linga did not require a concealed interior for its valuable adornment to be seized. Al-Biruni’s account identifies both the sacred form and the external wealth associated with it.

Ibn al-Athir’s later version says part of the object was burned and another portion carried to Ghazna. He also describes pillars, lamps, a golden chain with bells, and treasuries containing images of precious metal. These details place the sacred object within an elaborate institution; their architectural and numerical precision comes from that later source.[2]

The sum of treasure is another reported figure. The Elliot and Dowson translation of Ibn al-Athir says its value exceeded two million dinars. Other accounts and modern reconstructions print different sums. These cannot responsibly be converted into a single certain present-day cash value. The clear historical proposition is the seizure of substantial wealth, not an exact modern price tag.

Sacred fragments at Ghazna

The destruction was followed by transport and display. Al-Biruni says one portion lay in Ghazna’s hippodrome with the bronze Cakrasvamin from Thanesar. Another lay before the mosque door, where feet were cleaned on it. The placement converted a revered object into something to be trodden on.[1]

That detail makes humiliation a documented part of the outcome. The act was not simply the accidental damage of a building during a battle or the melting of metal to pay troops. A fragment retained its identity sufficiently for the conqueror’s public to understand what had been degraded. Material survival could be made to serve the message of religious defeat.

Al-Biruni’s tone is itself complex. He writes with extraordinary interest in Indian learning and records the destructive effect of Mahmud’s wars, yet also uses conventional prayers for the ruler. Readers should not flatten him into either a modern detached observer or an uncomplicated court propagandist. His testimony is valuable because it is specific and close to the period; it still requires interpretation.[1][4]

In his general discussion of the invasions, he says Mahmud ruined prosperity and scattered people, explaining that learning withdrew to regions such as Kashmir and Benares. This is a broad assessment of the damage visible to the scholar, not a claim that the whole subcontinent had been occupied or reduced to one condition.[4]

The return did not retrace a simple victory road

Taking Somnath did not remove Mahmud’s enemies or solve his supply problem. Later accounts describe a threatened interception by a ruler called Parama Dev. In the Tabaqat-i Akbari passage, Mahmud avoids that confrontation and returns through Sind toward Multan, suffering shortages of water and forage. The identity of Parama Dev has been debated; assigning him confidently to a particular famous king goes beyond this passage.[5]

Ibn al-Athir describes an operation against Bhima’s refuge, rendered Kandahat, involving a dangerous tidal crossing. He then takes Mahmud toward Mansura. Its ruler is called a Muslim apostate; he flees into date-palm country, where his followers are surrounded and many killed or drowned. The episode reminds us that Mahmud’s campaigning in this region also targeted Muslim opponents whom his historians condemned on doctrinal grounds.[6]

The return traditions also contain the story of a guide who deliberately leads the invaders into waterless country to avenge Somnath. A thirteenth-century version gives the guide a declaration of devotion, has him executed, and then describes a miraculous light guiding Mahmud’s army to water. The episode belongs to the history of remembered resistance and providential rescue. Its speeches and miracle cannot be treated as a contemporary transcript of the march.[5]

The broader hardship is better supported. Nazim’s analysis of Gardizi describes losses among men and animals and attacks by Jats along the retreat. The expedition’s final success at Ghazna therefore concealed a journey in which an army burdened with spoils remained vulnerable to thirst, unfamiliar routes, and local enemies.[3]

What happened after the army left?

The destruction of the image was not the same as establishing a durable Ghaznavid administration over Gujarat. Some much later stories describe Mahmud considering residence near Somnath or choosing a local ruler through elaborate court adventures. Nazim questions the evidence for a governor left there, and the accessible early testimony used here does not establish a permanent occupation regime.[3]

For the people and institutions affected, the army’s departure did not reverse the losses. Worship had been attacked, people killed, valuables removed, and a sacred object carried away for degradation abroad. Describing the expedition as a raid rather than a permanent annexation identifies its political form; it does not diminish its violence.

Nor should later restoration be used to erase the attack. Conversely, a photograph of the present Somnath temple should not be captioned as the building Mahmud saw. The present structure belongs to later reconstruction. Accurate images can show the coastal setting and the continuing importance of the site while making the difference in date clear.

A powerful later legend

The best-known story puts an offer of enormous ransom before Mahmud and has him choose fame as an idol-breaker rather than an idol-seller. A late version then rewards that apparent refusal of profit with jewels discovered inside the broken object. The story is dramatically satisfying precisely because it makes religious destruction and material gain harmonise perfectly.[5]

It is not verified speech from 1026. The late-sixteenth-century Tarikh-i Alfi, quoted by Elliot and Dowson, supplies an elaborate version; later authors repeat or develop it. Even the nineteenth-century editors point out the problem of hidden treasure inside a solid linga. The near-contemporary al-Biruni records precious external trappings, not this ransom exchange.[1][5]

The distinction matters because the legend can displace the harder history. The documented humiliation of fragments is already explicit. The later siege narrative already describes slaughter. Neither needs a fabricated royal quotation to make its moral or historical significance visible.

The campaign and its long memory

Somnath became one of the most powerful episodes in Mahmud’s reputation because a distant military expedition, a wealthy shrine, destruction of a sacred object, and a public claim of religious triumph converged. Its memory was then expanded by authors writing generations and centuries later. Their accounts preserve material worth examining, but their distance and purposes remain part of the story.

The evidential core is severe enough: Mahmud attacked Somnath, broke its linga, seized associated wealth, and sent fragments to Ghazna for degradation. The detailed later account adds sustained fighting, killings at the shrine, and deaths among those attempting escape. The reported totals remain uncertain, while the nature of the acts does not need to be concealed.[1][2]

Continue with the Jat campaign of 1027, whose reprisal tradition grows out of this difficult return, or compare the expedition with the other dossiers in the campaign guide.

title: Mahmud and the Jats, 1027: war on the Indus and the capture of families
excerpt: After the dangerous return from Somnath, Mahmud mounted a river campaign against the Jats. The sources describe spiked boats, drowning, killing and the seizure of families, while their enormous fleet totals remain doubtful.
html:
The army that returned from Somnath had carried away wealth and fragments of a sacred image, but its passage home was dangerous. Shortages, difficult country, and attacks by local opponents burdened the march. Among those opponents were Jats living in the Indus region. In 1027, according to the chronology reconstructed from Gardizi, Mahmud returned to punish them. The fighting this time centred on the river.[1]

The account is memorable for its boats armed with projecting iron spikes. Its human conclusion is more important: men drowned or were killed, refuges were searched, and the later chronicle explicitly describes the capture of families. This was a reprisal extending beyond a contest between armed crews. The violence reached people who had been sent away from the fighting in an effort to keep them safe.[1][2]

This is the final numbered dossier in the guide to Mahmud’s invasions, following the Somnath campaign of 1025–1026. It is often called his seventeenth invasion. That number is a conventional arrangement of campaigns, not a surviving contemporary catalogue. The river expedition can be examined on its own evidence without treating every traditional boundary and date as equally secure.

A reprisal rooted in the return from Somnath

The Somnath expedition did not end when the shrine was taken. Mahmud’s force had to return through western India and Sind, carrying possessions seized during the campaign. That movement exposed it to a different kind of struggle from an assault on a fortified religious centre. An army on the march needed water, forage, usable crossings, and enough protection for its people and animals.[1]

Gardizi, as analysed by Muhammad Nazim, describes Jat attacks during this difficult retreat. The late-sixteenth-century Tabaqat-i Akbari likewise explains the subsequent expedition as punishment for their interference with the returning army. The two traditions give the conflict a concrete cause: the invader’s withdrawal had been contested.[1][2]

Calling the Jats “raiders” or “rebels” without context would simply reproduce the victorious state’s perspective. People opposing an army passing through their region had their own interests, though the surviving accounts do not preserve their deliberations. Equally, a modern reconstruction cannot supply a speech in which they announce that they are avenging Somnath. The account records harassment and reprisal; its evidence for individual motives is much thinner.

The episode shows why possession of great booty did not automatically create security. A force successful at its distant objective could still be vulnerable where waterways, local knowledge, and dispersed opposition made a return route difficult. Mahmud’s next response sought to reverse that vulnerability by attacking opponents in their own river environment.

Who were the Jats in these accounts?

The medieval term identifies the communities targeted by the expedition, but it should not be turned into a complete description of every present-day Jat community. The sources concern particular people in a particular river region. They do not give us a census, a uniform political organisation, or the personal histories of their crews and families.

Older scholarship also produced uncertain geographical identifications. Elliot and Dowson called them Jats of Jud and connected them with the Salt Range. Nazim objects to that identification when analysing the river campaign. He also rejects a claim attributed through nineteenth-century scholarship that these Jats had forced the ruler of Mansura to abandon Islam, saying the statement lacks authority in the original text.[1][2]

These corrections matter because an incorrect starting place changes the entire military story. If the opponents are imagined as mountain people far from the river, their fleet appears inexplicable for one reason; if they are situated in the Indus environment described by the campaign, the practical setting is different. The safest account locates the fighting in the Indus region while leaving uncertain community geography visible.

There is also no need to make every opponent of Mahmud part of a single coordinated coalition. The sources describe campaigns against different rulers and communities, including Muslim opponents at Multan and Mansura. The Jat conflict belongs to that varied political landscape, even though court narratives fold many enemies into a single language of royal and religious victory.

Why 1027 rather than 1026?

The chronological issue has a specific answer in the scholarship. Nazim cites Gardizi for an expedition beginning in 418 AH, which he converts to March 1027, with a return at the beginning of summer. The later histories used in Elliot and Dowson generally give 417 AH instead. That lunar year overlaps parts of 1026 and 1027.[1][2]

An article that merely copies the old appendix can therefore move the expedition into the wrong year or make it seem an immediate continuation of the Somnath retreat. Nazim treats it as a renewed expedition after the return to Ghazna. He regards Gardizi as the crucial near-contemporary authority, rather than preferring the later date simply because several subsequent writers repeat it.[1]

The title follows the 1027 reconstruction. It does not suggest that the whole schedule can be recovered to the day from an official calendar. The distinction is enough to preserve the sequence: difficult retreat in 1026, then a campaign of punishment in the following year.

Preparing a force for the river

The expedition is associated with Multan as the place of preparation. The narrative describes an order to construct 1,400 boats, each equipped with iron projections: one forward and two at the sides. It also describes 20 archers assigned to each vessel and weapons including incendiary material.[1][2]

These figures are striking, but they remain reported figures. A fleet of that size would imply very substantial work in boatbuilding, timber, labour, crews, and supply. Elliot and Dowson considered the total implausible, while Nazim also expresses doubts about the size and the claimed effect of the spikes. Their scepticism does not remove the evidence for a river operation. It limits the confidence with which the account can be turned into a scale model.[1][2]

The older English translation uses the word “grenades.” In this context it should not evoke a modern explosive weapon. The passage places such missiles alongside naphtha, indicating incendiary warfare as understood by its translators. The exact construction of every projectile is not explained in the cited text.[2]

What the preparation makes clear is adaptation. The invader did not rely only on mounted troops pursuing opponents along a road. He sought a flotilla capable of engaging river craft and, in the version transmitted through Nazim, combined it with forces posted on the banks. The operation tried to deny escape by either water or land.

The Jat preparations and the island refuge

The opposing communities also prepared. The narrative says families and possessions were moved to an island or islands before the engagement. This was an attempt to separate those vulnerable people and valuable resources from the immediate battlefield.[1][2]

The sources give the opposing fleet immense totals. Nazim’s account reports 4,000 boats and immediately questions the figure. The Tabaqat-i Akbari version offers either 4,000 or 8,000. The disagreement is not a reason to choose 8,000 for dramatic effect. It is evidence that numerical enlargement and uncertain transmission shape the story.[1][2]

The types and sizes of these boats are not specified with enough precision to compare them with later ocean-going warships. A boat count is not automatically a count of vessels of equal size or equal fighting power. The account establishes a tradition of organised river resistance; it does not give the dimensions, tonnage, or crew lists needed for a technical reconstruction of the fleets.

Even without accepting the largest totals, the decision to move families away and prepare boats indicates that the opponents expected an attack of consequence. The river was both a means of resisting and a possible route of escape. Mahmud’s disposition aimed to control both uses.

Collision, arrows, and drowning

In the narrated battle, the flotillas meet and the projecting spikes damage the Jat boats that approach. Vessels overturn, men fall into the water, and the victors kill those who escape drowning. Nazim’s reconstruction adds bank detachments of mounted men supported by elephants, preventing fugitives from securing safety ashore.[1]

The spiked-boat mechanism is the account’s signature detail and one of its difficulties. A collision violent enough to overturn an opponent might also endanger the attacking vessel. Nazim notes the problem explicitly. We do not possess a contemporary drawing of the fittings or an archaeological discovery that resolves how they worked.[1]

That uncertainty should not make the human consequences disappear. The source tradition describes drowning, killing, and blocked escape, not simply the capture of abandoned boats. Its military triumph is represented through opponents trapped between water and forces on the banks. For those driven back from shore, the distinction between battle and attempted escape offered no protection.

There is no reliable total of dead. Thousands of boats, even if accepted, would not license multiplying an imagined standard crew into a casualty figure. The surviving narrative provides the nature of the violence and a claimed decisive defeat; it does not provide a verifiable body count.

The attack on the refuges

After the engagement, the victorious force proceeds to the places where people and property had been concealed. In Nazim’s account, many are killed and spoils captured. The Tabaqat-i Akbari passage explicitly says the families are taken prisoner.[1][2]

This is the campaign’s clearest extension beyond armed crews. A refuge chosen before battle becomes a target afterward. The story does not present women, children, and other family members as negotiating participants in a treaty; it presents them as people seized by the conquering force. Captivity was itself a form of violence, even where the text does not describe a captive being physically injured.

The later passage does not record the subsequent fate of every prisoner. It cannot establish exactly how many were enslaved, sold, ransomed, retained, or later released. Mahmud’s other campaigns include explicit slave sales, but those accounts do not supply a missing sale record for this expedition. The responsible statement here is that families were captured and exposed to the coercive power of their captors.

The word “spoils” can otherwise hide that distinction. Property could be carried away; a person could also be forced away from home. In a victory chronicle, both might contribute to the success of the expedition. A modern narrative should make the human content visible instead of allowing a conventional military term to conceal it.

Early testimony and later amplification

Elliot and Dowson believed the campaign was recorded only by later authorities. That judgment is outdated. Nazim’s work uses Gardizi’s near-contemporary account and cites a passing reference in the contemporary poet Farrukhi. The latter celebrates Mahmud through an image of hunting formidable creatures in the river; it confirms the place of the exploit in courtly praise but does not supply a detailed independent battle narrative.[1]

The more accessible Tabaqat-i Akbari passage remains useful because it preserves a complete translated version of the story, including the family captures. It should be identified as a late-sixteenth-century account rather than quoted as eyewitness testimony. The early Gardizi evidence is encountered here through Nazim’s source analysis; readers can distinguish that route of access from the directly available later translation.[1][2]

The combined evidence supports more than a vague rumour of a river fight, while leaving the enormous numbers and exact mechanics uncertain. It also prevents two opposite mistakes: dismissing the entire campaign because the old appendix doubts the fleet, or accepting every detail because an early writer mentions it. A near-contemporary court narrative can still exaggerate and celebrate.

What victory achieved

The accounts end with Mahmud returning to Ghazna. His opponents had suffered a defeat, property had been seized, and families had fallen into captivity. The reprisal demonstrated that attacks on his returning army could bring a separate campaign directed at the river communities themselves.[1][2]

The evidence does not establish the permanent destruction of every Jat community, the end of opposition throughout Sind, or a new administration over the whole Indus valley. A punitive expedition could be devastating without producing such sweeping political results. No later continuity of a community should be used to erase its losses, and no triumphal phrase should be converted into its total disappearance.

The campaign is frequently presented as the final item in Mahmud’s invasions of India. It was not the end of his reign, which continued until 1030, nor the end of Ghaznavid involvement in the subcontinent. Its place at the end of the familiar list reflects the way later histories organised his Indian campaigns.[1]

The cost hidden behind a final triumph

At the beginning of this sequence stood an army burdened by the return from Somnath. At its end stood a victorious reprisal narrative: damaged boats, men killed or drowned, refuges entered, and families captured. The river, briefly an environment in which local opponents had made the invader vulnerable, became the setting for an organised act of punishment.

The uncertain fleet totals should stay uncertain. The documented and reported forms of violence should stay visible. Together they produce a more useful history than either a perfectly engineered naval spectacle or a bloodless summary saying Mahmud “subdued the Jats.” Return to the campaign guide to compare this ending with the earlier battles, negotiated settlements, failed sieges, temple attacks, and forced movements of people that shaped his career.

Sources

title: Mahmud of Ghazni’s invasions of India: conquest, plunder, resistance, and the original sources
excerpt: A source-based guide to the seventeen conventionally counted campaigns, from the frontier and the Hindu Shahis to Mathura, Somnath, and the Indus: what contemporary writers report, what later chronicles add, and what remains uncertain.
html:
An army could leave Ghazna, defeat a king in the Punjab, seize elephants and captives, and return to Afghanistan without having conquered the country through which it had marched. It could come back to the same region years later because the earlier settlement had failed. It could strip a temple treasury while leaving a distant kingdom outside its permanent administration. These distinctions matter throughout the invasions of Mahmud of Ghazni, whose Indian campaigns between about 1000 and 1027 combined territorial expansion, tribute, religiously proclaimed warfare, enslavement, and the spectacular extraction of wealth. [1, 5]

The surviving sources describe killings, the taking and sale of captives, the burning of temples, and the removal and public degradation of sacred objects. Those acts belong plainly in the account. So do resistance, failed sieges, negotiated settlements, and the limits of the evidence. A court chronicler’s enormous casualty total is a claim to examine; a speech written centuries later is a tradition to date; a modern photograph of Somnath is a picture of a rebuilt temple. None should be quietly substituted for another. [1–5]

This guide brings together seventeen separate campaign articles. The numbering follows a familiar historical reconstruction, with combined operations identified and doubtful dates explained. It is a way of organizing the evidence, rather than a calendar handed down intact by an eleventh-century eyewitness. Each article follows the particular campaign, names the sources behind its claims, and distinguishes secure events from disputed identifications. [5, 6]

Who Mahmud was, and what “India” means here

Mahmud ruled from Ghazna, in present-day Afghanistan, from 998 to 1030. His dynasty emerged from the military and political world of the Samanids; his father, Sabuktigin, had already fought the Hindu Shahi ruler Jayapala. Mahmud inherited that frontier struggle while pursuing power across territories west and north of the Hindu Kush. His Indian expeditions formed one major part of a much wider reign. Ghazna was their imperial centre, their starting point, and the place to which many spoils and prisoners were carried. [1, 5, 6]

“India” in the sources refers to historical regions of the subcontinent, rather than the borders of the modern Republic of India. Peshawar, Hund, Multan, and Nandana are in present-day Pakistan; Ghazna is in Afghanistan; Mathura, Kannauj, Kalinjar, and Somnath are in present-day India. The frontier was a zone of competing states, defended crossings, mountain approaches, settlements, and commercial routes. Crossing a modern national boundary does not explain the political geography of 1001. [5, 6]

Nor was the subcontinent one state waiting to be defeated in a single battle. Hindu Shahi rulers, the Ismaili rulers of Multan, the rulers of Kashmir, the Pratiharas of Kannauj, Chandelas, and other regional powers faced different threats and made different decisions. Mahmud attacked Muslim opponents as well as Hindu ones. Multan is indispensable to this history precisely because it shows religious conflict within Islam alongside frontier rivalry, tribute, and strategic coercion. [1, 5]

The campaigns also had different outcomes. Ghaznavid power developed a lasting territorial base in the Punjab. Expeditions to the central Gangetic plain and the Gujarat coast were extraordinarily destructive but did not establish continuous Ghaznavid government over all those distant regions. Occupation, tributary submission, a successful raid, and the destruction of a sacred centre describe different kinds of power. [5, 6]

Why historians count seventeen campaigns

The confident phrase “seventeen invasions” conceals choices about what counts as an invasion. Should a revolt followed by a punitive march be listed separately? Should Waihind and Nagarkot count as one expedition or two? Should two attempts against Kashmir be distinguished when their accounts overlap? Can an undated river battle be securely attached to the campaign named in a later chronicle? [5]

Elliot and Dowson’s nineteenth-century compilation makes the problem unusually visible. Its Appendix, Note D, “Mahmud’s Expeditions to India,” begins by comparing totals that fail to match even the events their authors enumerate. It then arranges seventeen entries. That appendix is an editorial comparison of sources, including translated passages, rather than an eleventh-century chronicle in its own right. Its colonial judgments and geographical guesses need scrutiny alongside the courtly language of the medieval texts it reproduces. [5]

This series uses that seventeen-entry framework while incorporating chronological corrections and retaining uncertainty. The Sukhpal episode begins with revolt in late 1007 and the response in early 1008. Nandana belongs to 1013–14; the first Kashmir operation extended across 1015–16. The Chandela and Rahib narratives are difficult to align. The Jat expedition is conventionally dated 1027, although the late narrative printed by Elliot and Dowson gives a Hijri year spanning parts of 1026 and 1027. Dates spanning two years may describe a campaigning season or the conversion of a lunar year, rather than two separate invasions. [5, 6]

The campaign sequence

The links below lead to complete individual accounts. A date qualified as “traditional” or “disputed” should remain qualified when the episode is retold.

Part Date used in this series Campaign and principal issue
1 About 1000 Frontier operations: the small opening expedition and the limits of its documentation.
2 1001 Peshawar and Jayapala: battle, royal captivity, ransom, and the Shahi succession.
3 1004–05 Bhatia: resistance, pursuit, plunder, and a disputed location.
4 1005–06, conventionally 1006 The first Multan campaign: an Ismaili ruler, Shahi resistance, and submission.
5 1007–08 Sukhpal’s revolt: the collapse of an imposed political and religious settlement.
6 1008–09 Waihind and Nagarkot: a dangerous battle followed by the seizure of a hill-fort treasury.
7 1009 Narayan: destruction, tribute, and commercial passage; its location remains disputed.
8 1010 The second Multan campaign: renewed coercion and the removal of the earlier ruler.
9 1013–14 Nandana: the Salt Range, Shahi resistance, and captives taken to Ghazna.
10 1014–15 Thanesar: the attack on a sacred centre and the removal of Cakrasvamin.
11 1015–16 The first Kashmir expedition: a failed siege and the constraints of weather and terrain.
12 1018–19 Mathura and Kannauj: temple destruction, plunder, fighting, and mass captivity in the Gangetic plain.
13 1019–20 preferred; later dating disputed The Chandela and Rahib campaign: a river crossing and narratives that cannot be aligned without reservation; Gardizi, as discussed by Nazim, supports the earlier chronology.
14 1021–22 Kashmir and Lahore: a second failed Kashmir attempt and the extension of power in the Punjab.
15 1022–23 Gwalior and Kalinjar: strongholds, elephants, and negotiated peace.
16 1025–26 Somnath: a distant coastal shrine, destruction supported by near-contemporary testimony, and a difficult return.
17 Traditionally 1027 The Jat expedition: reprisals on the Indus, early testimony transmitted through scholarship, and disputed fleet totals.

From the Shahi frontier to the Punjab

The early campaigns arose from a conflict already under way before Mahmud became ruler. Sabuktigin’s fighting with Jayapala had weakened the Shahi position; Mahmud carried the struggle forward. The small expedition conventionally placed in 1000 is much less fully documented than the confrontation outside Peshawar in 1001. Treating them as equally well observed would conceal an important difference in the record. [1, 5, 6]

For Peshawar, al-Utbi supplies a narrative of battle, Jayapala’s capture with relatives, the stripping of jewels, demands for elephants and ransom, and release under humiliating conditions. He goes on to describe Jayapala’s death by self-immolation. This is a victor’s account, shaped to magnify Mahmud’s triumph. It nevertheless gives a concrete picture of conquest working through captured rulers, material exactions, and compelled political agreements. The enormous totals of dead and captives in the same passage cannot be treated as independently verified statistics. [1, pp. 24–27]

Bhatia illustrates both the violence of resistance and the practical limits of victory. Al-Utbi describes the ruler Bijai Rai resisting, withdrawing under pressure, and killing himself when pursued; the account includes killing, seizure of elephants, and the establishment of a religious instructor. It also records an uncomfortable return during the rains, with baggage lost in swollen rivers. The chronicler’s triumphal narrative contains evidence of logistical danger. Bhatia’s identification with Bhera or Bathinda is disputed, so a modern monument at either place cannot by itself authenticate the campaign’s route. [1, pp. 28–30; 5, 6]

The struggle over Multan was different. Its Ismaili ruler was a Muslim opponent whom the Ghaznavid source represented as both politically disobedient and religiously heretical. Mahmud also fought Anandapala after being refused passage through Shahi territory. Submission, financial penalties, and changes of authority did not settle the region permanently: Sukhpal’s revolt and the later return to Multan reveal the instability of arrangements that a victory announcement might make sound final. [1, pp. 30–33; 5]

At Waihind in 1008–09, al-Utbi’s account acknowledges that the Ghaznavids came close to defeat before an attack by Mahmud’s household troops helped turn the battle. Later narratives tell the famous story of panic beginning with an elephant; that version should be introduced as later testimony, rather than inserted into the contemporary account without explanation. The distinction matters because military success depended on contingencies, rather than an inevitable superiority established before the armies met. [1, pp. 33–34; 5]

The seizure of Nagarkot’s accumulated wealth then provided a different sort of victory. Al-Utbi describes a fortress opening its gates in fear, officials taking charge of treasures, and the spoils subsequently displayed at Ghazna before envoys. His vast fiscal totals celebrate imperial abundance. The surrender described in this passage does not justify inventing a prolonged storming or a massacre within the fort. The documented extraction of devotional wealth is itself a substantial event. [1, pp. 34–35]

Sacred centres, tribute, and the reach of the army

Narayan, Nandana, and Thanesar are easy to confuse when older translations render unfamiliar place names differently. They are separate entries in this series. Narayan’s location is disputed; Nandana belongs to the Salt Range and the struggle with the Shahis; Thanesar was a major sacred centre whose removed image is independently mentioned by al-Biruni. Similar-looking names in a modern transcription do not establish that they are one event. [1, pp. 36–41; 3; 5, 6]

The Narayan passage is particularly revealing about the combination of violence and negotiated interest. Al-Utbi describes defeat, killing, the overthrow of images, and plunder, followed by arrangements involving elephants, manpower, and the safe movement of caravans between Hind and Khurasan. Destruction and commercial passage appear within the same account. A campaign could aim to break resistance and then obtain resources or security through an agreement. [1, p. 36]

Nandana’s campaign narrative adds snow, obstructed movement, fighting in a pass, pursuit, and the taking of many captives. Al-Utbi describes the subsequent cheapness of prisoners in the conqueror’s market. That claim turns the reader’s attention from the ruler’s battlefield triumph to the people converted into saleable property. Captivity was an economic result of war as well as an emblem of domination. The text preserves the victor’s view of the market; it does not preserve the names or subsequent lives of most of those sold. [1, pp. 37–39]

At Thanesar, the destruction and removal of a sacred object can be followed beyond the campaign narrative. Al-Biruni identifies the bronze Cakrasvamin from Thanesar at Ghazna, beside material taken from Somnath. His statement is a near-contemporary witness to the relocation and humiliating display of sacred objects. It is stronger evidence for that particular claim than an unexamined succession of later chronicles repeating the same story. [1, pp. 40–41; 3, ch. XI, p. 117]

Kashmir supplies a necessary corrective to accounts in which every march ends in effortless conquest. The expeditions conventionally placed in 1015–16 and 1021–22 did not open the valley to permanent Ghaznavid conquest. Defended approaches, the fort associated with Lohkot, weather, provisions, and retreat all belong to their history. The chronology of the two operations has itself been debated. The more durable extension of authority in the Punjab should not be converted into a claim that Kashmir also fell. [5, 6]

Mathura and Kannauj: admiration followed by destruction

The expedition of 1018–19 carried Mahmud’s army into the Gangetic plain. Al-Utbi’s account follows river crossings, submissions, fighting, the destruction of sacred buildings, and the capture and dispersal of people. It is among the fullest contemporary narratives available for the series, although its rhetorical numbers and identifications still require examination. [1, pp. 41–50; 2, ch. XLIX]

At Mathura, the account attributes to Mahmud a striking appreciation of the scale and workmanship of the city’s temples. That admiration did not protect them. The text then reports an order for temples to be burned with naphtha and levelled. Architectural admiration and deliberate destruction coexist in the source; quoting the first while omitting the second would misrepresent the sequence. Conversely, the attributed letter and extravagant estimates of construction costs should not become a modern architectural survey. [1, pp. 44–45]

The same expedition involved different kinds of coercion at different places. Al-Utbi describes conversion and submission under threat at Baran, fighting and death around Kulchand’s stronghold, plunder and captivity at Kannauj, and further violence at Asi and Sharwa. The identity of the Kannauj ruler is complicated by the names transmitted in the sources. A continuous literary narrative must not make every place identification or royal name appear equally secure. [1, pp. 42–49]

Its conclusion is explicit about enslaved people. The chronicler says captives were sold and carried toward regions including Khurasan, Iraq, and Transoxiana, giving very low reported prices. Those figures express the scale of the victory as the author wished to present it; they are not a surviving set of market accounts. The underlying practice is clear: human beings were among the commodities extracted by the campaign. A catalogue limited to gold, silver, and elephants would leave out one of its most consequential forms of plunder. [1, p. 50]

Later expeditions toward Chandela power, Gwalior, and Kalinjar require a more cautious reconstruction. The undated Rahib battle in al-Utbi does not simply give us all the protagonists and motives found in much later accounts. In the Kalinjar narrative printed from the Tabaqat-i Akbari, elephants and peace are central to the settlement. It describes negotiation; calling it the storming and occupation of an impregnable fortress would exceed even that later account. [1, pp. 50–51; 5, pp. 462–468]

Somnath: what the earliest evidence establishes

The attack on Somnath in 1025–26 became the most famous of Mahmud’s Indian expeditions. Its fame has also accumulated episodes and speeches of very different dates. The first task is to distinguish the near-contemporary evidence from the expanded narratives and moral anecdotes written later. Alongside al-Biruni, Gardizi and the poet Farrukhi preserve early material on the expedition and its return, discussed here through Nazim’s source comparison. The extended siege narrative quoted below comes from the much later Ibn al-Athir. Al-Utbi’s surviving Indian campaign narrative does not reach this expedition. Citing him for Somnath would therefore give a false impression of contemporary corroboration. [1, 2, 4–6]

Al-Biruni provides a firm starting point. In India, volume II, chapter LVIII, he dates the destruction of Somnath’s image to 416 AH. He describes the upper part being broken, the remainder carried to Ghazna with valuable coverings and ornaments, and portions placed at the hippodrome and the mosque entrance. He identifies the sacred object as a linga of Mahadeva. This testimony supports destruction, seizure, transportation, and deliberate humiliation. It does not supply a death toll or a transcript of an exchange about ransom. [4, p. 103]

His following pages also place Somnath within a coastal and religious world. He relates its fame to maritime travel and its harbour, describes offerings and beliefs, and discusses its situation near the Sarasvati’s mouth. These observations help explain why the site mattered beyond the wealth it contained. Somnath was a place of worship and a landmark in a wider geography of movement, patronage, and reputation. [4, pp. 104–105]

The extended account reproduced from Ibn al-Athir was written roughly two centuries later. It describes the desert approach, assaults, fighting around the temple, killing, and the breaking of the sacred object. Its reported totals of more than 50,000 slain and enormous treasure must remain attributed figures. The account’s chronological discrepancy in the printed edition is another reason to anchor the date in al-Biruni rather than silently combine every detail into a seamless eyewitness narrative. [5, pp. 468–471]

The famous claim that Mahmud chose to be an “idol-breaker” rather than an “idol-seller” belongs to later elaborations of a ransom story. The version in which jewels pour from a broken image presents additional problems when compared with al-Biruni’s description of a linga. Readers can study how such stories developed without treating them as recorded speech. Their dramatic appeal does not make them contemporary evidence. [4, p. 103; 5, pp. 471–476]

The return was also part of the campaign. Later sources describe threatened interception, movement through Sind, water and forage shortages, and attacks in the lower Indus region. They differ about names, routes, and narrative details. The famous story of a deliberately misleading guide and miraculous rescue is a later religious narrative, rather than a route survey. The army’s ability to reach a distant shrine did not remove the hazards of getting its men, animals, and spoils home. [5, pp. 473–475]

The Indus reprisals and the limits of a final victory

The last conventionally counted expedition concerns Jat communities on the Indus, said to have attacked Mahmud’s army during the return from Somnath. A much later narrative describes boats built at Multan, iron projections, archers and incendiaries, fighting against opposing craft, drowning and killing, and the capture of families concealed on islands. Its treatment of families makes the violence extend beyond a contest between armed crews. [5, pp. 477–478]

The spectacular fleet totals in that account should not be turned into modern naval statistics. Elliot and Dowson themselves express serious doubts about the scale, but their claim that only late authorities recorded the expedition is outdated. Nazim cites the near-contemporary Gardizi for the river operation and its boats, weapons, and archers, and dates it to March 1027 in 418 AH. Gardizi is consulted here through that scholarly discussion, rather than a newly checked direct translation. The earlier strand strengthens the case for the campaign without independently validating every fleet total or mechanical detail. The dating and scale problems belong alongside the described punitive violence. [5, 6]

This final episode also changes the perspective on the preceding victory. Populations along a returning army’s route could threaten its movement. Control of a great treasury did not guarantee control of river channels, landing places, provisions, or local communities. The account of reprisals represents Ghaznavid power answering such resistance; it does not prove that resistance had been impossible or that the entire Indus region could be managed through one battle. [5]

Religion, wealth, and political power in the sources

Religious purpose is explicit in the Ghaznavid court narrative. Al-Utbi links Mahmud’s programme to holy war, celebrates the defeat of non-Muslim rulers and the destruction of images, and treats the suppression of Multan’s Ismailis as a religious achievement. Those statements should be read as evidence of the monarchy’s proclaimed legitimacy. Removing religion from the account would discard a language through which campaigns were justified and triumphs displayed. [1, pp. 24, 30–41]

The same passages repeatedly concern money, elephants, captives, tribute, appointments, and routes. Religious hostility and material extraction could reinforce each other. A temple could be attacked as a sacred institution, stripped of accumulated valuables, and made into evidence of the conqueror’s triumph at home. A defeated ruler might survive after surrendering resources. A subordinate could be retained or replaced according to the political settlement. The sources support examining these mechanisms together, rather than assigning one exclusive motive to every expedition. [1, 5]

Ghazna’s display of captured wealth made victory visible to audiences far from the battlefield. Al-Utbi describes the exhibition of Nagarkot’s treasure, the market in captives, and monumental building in the capital. Al-Biruni describes sacred objects placed where they could be exposed to public degradation. The journey of a captured object or person thus continued after the army left the place it had attacked. It helped turn distant violence into imperial prestige and resources. [1, pp. 34–35, 50; 2, ch. L; 3, 4]

The human consequences cannot be measured simply by repeating the largest number in a chronicle. Al-Biruni’s opening discussion of India associates Mahmud’s wars with ruined prosperity, dispersal, deepened hostility, and the retreat of learning toward places such as Kashmir and Benares. It is a broad, near-contemporary assessment with its own perspective and generalizations, rather than a census of every region. It belongs beside the triumphant court narrative because it records a different understanding of what conquest had done. [3, ch. I, p. 22]

How to read the original sources

Al-Utbi was close to the Ghaznavid political world. His Kitab al-Yamini is foundational for the early campaigns and the expedition to Mathura and Kannauj. Proximity gives the work value but does not turn its praise, casualty totals, speeches, or religious polemic into neutral reporting. The English editions used here also have a history: Reynolds’s 1858 translation works through a medieval Persian version of the Arabic chronicle, while Elliot and Dowson provide selected translated extracts with editorial notes. Wording should be checked against the particular edition cited. [1, 2]

Al-Biruni, writing about India around 1030, offers a different kind of evidence: scholarly description, geography, religious explanation, and observations about the effects of conquest. His remarks on the Thanesar and Somnath objects are especially important. He is not a full campaign diarist, and his proximity to the period does not make him an eyewitness of every action. [3, 4]

Gardizi provides another near-contemporary strand used in scholarly reconstruction of the chronology. In this guide, claims that depend on its comparison with other sources are identified through Muhammad Nazim’s source-critical study. A scholarly citation to Gardizi is not silently presented as a fresh direct translation of a manuscript. This is particularly important where campaign dates in older compilations have been corrected. [6]

Ibn al-Athir, Minhaj-i Siraj, Nizam al-Din Ahmad, and Firishta wrote at differing distances from Mahmud’s lifetime, extending from roughly two centuries to about six centuries after the campaigns. They preserve valuable traditions, and sometimes material unavailable elsewhere, but their accounts are not interchangeable contemporary witnesses. Repetition among dependent narratives does not create several independent confirmations. Later speeches and precise figures need the author’s name and date beside them. [5, 6]

The result is a history with different degrees of resolution. We can speak directly about the killing, enslavement, temple destruction, extraction, and sacred-object humiliation attested in particular sources. We can also say plainly when a location, date, head count, itinerary, or dramatic anecdote remains uncertain. The seventeen articles that follow keep both kinds of statement visible, so readers can follow the campaigns and examine the evidence on which their reconstruction rests.
